In this research, a time series approach was employed with a copula to account for potential non-stationarity, and a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method was used for Bayesian parameter estimation. The proposed model was evaluated using simulated data and an experimental setup, and the results showed good agreement with the actual values and indicated that the model can effectively estimate parameters and observe trends in data, even with low samples sizes commonly found in wave engineering. The research was further validated through an analysis of real world data in the North Sea, and the results were comparable to established methods including the Beta and Bayesian approaches. The novel model produced a lower RMSE in prediction, indicating its potential for use in wave energy converter design and other offshore applications. The model has been made available online for the benefit of the wave engineering community.

This paper presents an approach to accurately capturing the meaning of word pairs in embeddings, specifically addressing the frequent issue of antonyms being mapped to synonyms. We develop a novel technique for generating clean datasets and a method to update embeddings to reflect the intended relationships between words. Our proposal incorporates a quality control measure to ensure the validity of constructed pairs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to financial text and utilizing it to update popular embedding methods. Our results indicate that our technique surpasses comparative methods in accuracy and achieves a substantial improvement in modeling intended meanings. We also introduce an additional technique to proactively identify and mitigate the mapping of antonyms to synonyms in embeddings.

In this letter, we address the challenges of designing waveforming strategies that minimize interference in wideband applications and maximize fair-throughput/sum-throughput performance. To tackle this issue, we frame it as an optimization problem and leverage convex optimization techniques to derive efficient solutions, leveraging the properties of polynomial matrix invariants to simplify the problem formulation. To accommodate practical considerations and robust performance, we also explore robust waveforming strategies and provide these solutions as well. To validate our theoretical findings, we include relevant numerical examples and computational results.

A complete dynamic model for the onset of Rayleigh--B\'enard instability in a horizontal box filled with an viscous fluid is created, addressing the limitations of previous studies. Prior work neglected the impact of lateral boundary conditions on the development of instability near the box's center, while also skewing the detected patterns. Additionally, earlier numerical implementations relied on simplified models for modeling the development of instability, which failed to capture the full dynamics of the instability's early stages. Our model utilizes a novel "pseudospectral" implementation of the Navier-Stokes equations that considers the effects of both lateral boundary conditions and the development of the instability in the fluid's interior, ultimately successfully reproducing the iconic "cellular" patterns of the Rayleigh--B\'enard instability.

A enduring challenge in natural language processing and computational linguistics lies in capturing the underlying universal grammar that underpins human language. Noam Chomsky's Minimalist Program offers a theoretical framework for this endeavor, but it also introduces complex and loosely defined concepts that are difficult to apply computationally. To overcome this obstacle, the authors present a novel way to analyze linguistic structures using a graph-based representation and substructure identification. This method converts the search for a suitable derivation into a more manageable substructure identification task within a pre-established linguistic framework, thus making it feasible to employ computational methods for search and optimization. By leveraging this approach, the authors successfully demonstrate the solution of various previously insurmountable problems in linguistic analysis, such as resolving action sequences and reordering transformations. Furthermore, this method facilitates the resolution of ambiguous derivations by prioritizing certain features over others in a logically consistent manner, inspired by the Minimalist Program's concept of Merge.

In collaborative settings, players must learn to reject actions that lead to worse outcomes through a chain reaction, often requiring a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics. This challenge becomes even more complex in environments beyond simple examples, such as when there are numerous agents, various action spaces, or limited observation capabilities. To tackle this issue, we present a novel algorithm that allows agents to identify and avoid these interconnected, detrimental effects by learning a more accurate predictive model of the environment's behavior. By doing so, they can anticipate the consequences of their actions and shape the outcome of the game in their favor. We evaluated the effectiveness of this approach by testing it against a variety of difficult cases, including scenarios involving multiple agents, large action spaces, and partial observation, and found that it consistently outperformed alternative methods.

In an emerging model of temporal network evolution, individuals' connections change in a random, asynchronous manner, leading to a potential crisis in defining time in the network, especially since standard methods fail to account for the inherent synchrony issues inherent to its non-deterministic, asynchronous nature. This time-entanglement crisis prompts researchers to reevaluate their understanding of time's role and whether it even remains a relevant concept in such complex systems. A simple epidemic model is then utilized as a case study to demonstrate the challenges of determining the impact of connection changes on the spread of disease, with the resulting data revealing a near-universal increase in the number of individuals infected as the network is modified to operate in a more asynchronous manner. Furthermore, the model highlights the difficulties of accurately defining the timing of infection due to the inherent synchrony issues present in the network, ultimately leading to the conclusion that the concept of time must be reexamined in complex systems to prevent the implicit adoption of biased methods that skew results.

We examine Cotton solitons in $3$-manifolds, particularly those with the Reeb vector field whose orthogonal space contains a closed, self-orthogonal null vector. We demonstrate that this special geometry is associated with the steady Cotton soliton and prove the uniqueness of such solitons in the mentioned context. Additionally, we prove that the soliton's potential vector field is parallel when the associated Reeb flow has an infinite period.

A Python library for computing and fitting parton distribution functions has been developed as part of the xFitter framework. This library, known as Melas, allocates tasks to multiple CPUs for the global analysis of data sets at varying scales, incorporating the DGLAP evolution through an iterative process. As a result, Melas can handle a comprehensive range of tasks, including the fitting of parameters, calculating the DGLAP evolution, integrating functions across scales, solving inverse problems, and determining the uncertainty through bootstrap methods. By leveraging the DGLAP evolution, Melas can significantly reduce the computational time required for the fit by narrowing down the search range before employing an iterative method. Additionally, Melas features an efficient way to handle experimental constraints and uncertainty propagation through bootstrapping, which can be applied to various fit functions, even those that are not linear. As the underlying code is straightforward and well-documented, Melas serves as an ideal teaching tool for introducing students to the DGLAP evolution, PDF fitting, and associated computational techniques through hands-on experience.

To minimize the negative impact of using experience replay in reinforcement learning, we introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework that minimizes the variance of the policy gradient estimation in a batch setting. The proposed algorithm iteratively generates new data, updates the experience replay buffer, and derives a theoretically optimal variance-reduced estimator. The algorithm's effectiveness is verified through experiments on multiple benchmark problems.

The libcommute library of Python 2 modules is now upgraded to support Python 3,  no longer relying on the old Python Numeric and NumPy libraries for its core functionality. This revision includes numerous new features such as customizable string representations for states and operators, state sorting capabilities, selective unitary conjugation, and the ability to create operator strings from commuting patterns. Additionally, its convergence checker can now handle unitary approximations and is part of the rebranded "utils" module.

Using high-resolution ARPES at the Ti-1080 beamline of the PFAS at the Institute of Nuclear Energy Research, we employed a combination of initial and modified band structures of Ba(Fe$_{0.92}$Co$_{0.08}$)$_2$As$_2$ to investigate the superconducting gap anisotropy via angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Notably, we observed a significant anisotropy of the superconducting gap, with an estimated value of $\frac{\Delta_{\Gamma}}{\Delta_{M}}\approx2.5$, which is notably larger than previous measurements in iron-based superconductors, notably in CaKFe$_4$As$_4$ with a ratio of approximately 1.5, but consistent with theoretical models that indicate a gap anisotropy of approximately 3 or greater around the zone corner. Additionally, our results utilizing modified band structures reveal a nodal line at the M point within the superconducting state, which is in alignment with recent theoretical predictions.

We establish a direct link between the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula by applying the bosonization method for supercharges. Furthermore, this connection enables us to extend the superbosonization formula to more complex Hamiltonian operators, such as those involving higher-order derivatives and interacting with fermionic fields in external magnetic and chemical potentials fields.

Initial findings from the LHCb experiment's first top quark production data reveal a higher measured spin asymmetry than predicted by the standard model, a significant discrepancy of approximately 3.5 sigma. To verify this result, the LHCb experiment repeated the same analysis using full ATLAS and CMS data sets from 7 and 8 TeV proton-proton collisions. Combining all relevant results from ATLAS and CMS, including additional systematic uncertainties, significantly reduces the deviation from the standard model prediction, from 3.2 sigma to 2.0 sigma.

LaNiO$_3$ superlattices with varying LaNiO$_3$ thickness were investigated, specifically the LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices from one period to 10 periods. Our findings show that the conductive component in LaNiO$_3$ exhibits significant temperature dependence, displaying both fast relaxing and slow components. The fast relaxing component's temperature dependence varies substantially with LaNiO$_3$ thickness, exhibiting an apparent shift in activation energy from approximately 0.26 eV in one-period samples to 0.17 eV in 10-period samples. Additionally, the slow component's temperature dependence aligns with that of LaAlO$_3$ but only becomes dominant in 10-period samples, suggesting that the LaNiO$_3$ conductive component's slow behavior might be masked by the fast relaxing component for thinner films.

To understand how machine learning models for natural language processing portray entities with mental states and the potential for deception, we developed two tests mimicking the theory of mind concept from psychology. One test assesses the ability of a model to generate dialogue while considering the knowledge that another entity will share information with others, though intentionally hiding some part of it. The other test involves a model that must produce dialogue while being aware of its own future capacity for either truthful or dishonest behavior in a given context. We applied these tests to evaluate various models, including both human-led and human-interacting systems, in a controlled virtual environment involving three roles: a knowledge holder, a communicator, and a recipient. Our findings showed that advanced language models are capable of predicting aspects of entities' mental states and sometimes even their own future capabilities, but they struggle with accurately forecasting their own intentions and the entities' intentions to either tell the truth or lie.

In this study, we examine the average capacity of a wireless communication system that uses the capabilities of large intelligent surfaces, which can dynamically adjust the reflection coefficients of multiple independent fading channels. We first establish the distribution of the capacity weights, which are the squared values of the reflected signal strengths, and then derive the related moment generating function. By utilizing this information, we are able to determine the ergodic capacity of the SISO-RIS communication system and optimize it by varying the RIS's phase shifts. Our findings indicate that when the RIS is far from both transmitter and receiver, the optimal solution involves setting the corresponding reflection coefficient to the one with the strongest impact on enhancing the received signal's strength, thus effectively converting a complex multi-channel system into a simpler single-channel system with enhanced signal quality.

MG-GLAM, the most recent iteration of the Hennesy-Gullud-Hennsey code, is an open-source, high-performance computational tool developed for time-dependent N-body simulations in general relativity. Based on the time-domain unpolarized perturbation theory for gravitational waves, MG-GLAM calculates quadratic gravitational waves emitted by three distinct object interactions. The code's latest version includes improvements to handle binary supermassive black hole mergers with surrounding stellar clusters, specifically dealing with wave generation during such events. Building upon the successful integration of the Einstein Telescope's observable model, the MG-GLAM framework now offers a versatile framework for calculating detectable sources of gravitational waves in complex astrophysical environments.

We demonstrate that the chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE$_\kappa$ for $\kappa\in(4,\infty)$) surfaces can be represented as a collection of discrete, disconnected planar regions within a complex plane, coupled with a process that changes these surfaces over time. This shows that SLE$_\kappa$ consists of growing "imaginary wings" originating from the initial trace, and can also be viewed as the evolution of a tree-decomposed domain under mass removal. The analysis provides a connection between the Loewner equation and the Schramm-Loewner evolution, and enables the derivation of new scaling relations for planar graphs and their corresponding scaling limits.

This paper introduces WorkingWiki, a sophisticated version of the typical wiki platform designed for collaborative software development and manuscript publication. By integrating issue tracking, version control, and collaborative writing tools from Atlassian's Confluence and Bitbucket, WorkingWiki offers a unified platform for managing software and scientific projects. Its unique features in WorkingWiki include customizable workflows, macro capabilities for embedded tools, and advanced permission settings, which can be tailored to control both wiki content and attached software. To further enhance collaboration, WorkingWiki incorporates built-in support for real-time co-editing, @mentions, and commenting on specific text sections. Additionally, it provides a search function, macro libraries, and app extensions for extended functionality.

This study involves enhancing the linearized model of turbulent reactive flows by utilizing the double-delta function combustion model. We demonstrate that by assuming equilibrium and incorporating the Edwards-Baldry model, this model can be adapted to the linearized framework. We further derive a simplified surface density flux model by analyzing the double-delta function combustion model, and validate it against the joint probability density function approach for various scenarios, including different Damkoehler numbers and equilibrium surface densities.

Researchers studying oscillations in stars have found a crucial role for the acoustic-buoyant frequency in their wave behaviors. When this frequency matches the break frequency, where the star's wave resistance suddenly changes, a shock wave forms, leading to a drastic shift in wave behavior. A recent model reveals that the acoustic-buoyant frequency arises from the interplay between the star's internal waves and its surface layers, specifically where the wave resistance meets the requirements for stability. In this explanation, the acoustic-buoyant frequency is directly tied to the break frequency, which is determined by the specific properties of the stable layers, such as their viscosity and density.

A continuous, expanded approach has been developed to identify the number of distinct patterns of cluster synchronization occurring within a nonlinear network. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through analyses of a fractional-order Chua circuit network and a linear network containing multiple interactions between groups. The proposed approach enables the derivation of conditions that ensure the existence, as well as the location, of the cluster synchronization regime in the network. This is achieved without needing to solve a large number of nonlinear equations. Instead, the focus is on determining the number of cluster trajectories by analyzing a reduced set of linear equations. This can be done more efficiently than solving the original nonlinear dynamics for each individual cluster. As a result, this approach provides a more efficient way to study cluster synchronization.

We examine the behavior of nearest-neighbor coupled dynamical units on two specific spatial configurations, the triadic and diamond lattices, which have not been extensively studied previously. By applying dimer dynamics as a model, we explore the impact of these geometries on symmetry and phase transitions, and our findings reveal that the triadic lattice exhibits a diverse range of symmetry patterns while the diamond lattice does not. Moreover, our simulation demonstrates that the triadic lattice undergoes a continuous transition in symmetry, which is also present in the dimer model, albeit with distinct temperature dependence, and can be influenced by the coupling of pairs of dynamos that are two lattice sites apart.

We investigate the consequences of ultralight dark matter being coupled to neutrinos, a scenario that could be revealed by current neutrino oscillation experiments or forthcoming ones. The interplay between this coupling and the neutrino dispersion due to gravitational effects then becomes significant in the early universe. As a result, a quantum cosmological perturbation theory yields a novel, neutrino-dominated expression for the power spectrum of the curvature spectrum. Furthermore, we find that even tiny dark matter masses can produce distinct features in the power spectrum, located at very large scales corresponding to the matter horizon crossing during the ultralight dark matter period of oscillations.

Extremely energetic cosmic photons, which could originate from powerful beacons such as the Great Attractor, may generate extensive cosmic ray ensembles when interacting with a massive object's gravitational field. These cosmic rays, which could encompass a significant portion of the electromagnetic spectrum from gamma rays to low-energy particles, may be produced through the acceleration of particles as they are bent back on a curved path by the gravitational force. A key aspect of these ensembles is how they might be distinguished from conventional cosmic ray events, which involves considering both the spatial characteristics of the particles and the energy they carry. A potential indicator of photo-generated ensembles could be the presence of extremely long cosmic ray tracks that span across the Contour-7 surface, which is defined by the detection apparatus of a specific cosmic ray experiment. These tracks, which could be produced by particles that traverse a particularly large distance through the Earth, may provide a key to identifying photo-generated ensembles and, by extension, pinpointing the sources of these extremely energetic photons.

A fundamental issue in nonlocal gravity theory has been addressed, and we believe the solution is both straightforward and compelling. The problem centered on the nonlocal theory's constitutive relation, which had varying representations, and we contend that it should be based solely on the nonlocal curvature in the four-dimensional spacetime, independently of the number of spatial dimensions. This viewpoint leads to a specific relation that directly connects the nonlocal gravity component to the nonlocal scalar curvature, which in turn results in the nonlocal gravity component being directly proportional to the nonlocal scalar curvature, and since the nonlocal scalar curvature is essentially the nonlocal Ricci scalar divided by the nonlocal gravitational constant, this relation effectively redefines the nonlocal gravitational constant in terms of the nonlocal Ricci scalar, which then implies that the nonlocal gravitational constant is equivalent to the product of the nonlocal Einstein constant and the nonlocal spatial compaction length squared, which in turn enables the nonlocal Einstein constant to be expressed as the nonlocal gravitational constant divided by the nonlocal spatial compaction length squared. This expression has significant implications for understanding nonlocal gravity and its connection to the deformed phase space theory.

Autonomous distributed systems require a special type of data structure whose updates converge automatically, ensuring consistency and safety.  Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) have emerged as a prominent solution for these applications, ensuring that all replicas of data reach a consistent state.  However, as the use of CRDTs becomes more widespread, there is a growing need for a design framework to specify and formally verify the properties of these data structures.  This paper presents such a design framework, based on a novel combination of existing techniques from distributed systems and formal verification.  By integrating the specifications of CRDTs with a novel saturation predicate, this framework can automatically prove that a given data structure indeed converges to a consistent state.  This is achieved without relying on a specific implementation of the data structure's replica, but rather through a theoretical demonstration of its properties.  This design framework has already successfully verified the convergence of several well-known CRDTs, including Last-Seen CRDT, Vector CRDT, Counting CRDT, and Distributed Transaction CRDT.

We examined 9800+ phenotypes associated with 3 million+ protein-coding variants, looking at how protein sequences influence the incidence of these variants. Our data shows that for the majority of traits, the impact of protein sequence is minimal. However, for around 2000 phenotypes, the incidence of variants is significantly affected by the specific amino acid present, with some affecting multiple traits. Our analysis reveals that the connection between protein sequence and the incidence of variants with functional consequences is complex, shaped by factors like the specific location within a protein and the effects of co-evolving residues. Moreover, we found that around 10% of variants with functional consequences are linked to particular amino acids that have a significant impact on the stability, activity, or interaction properties of the resulting protein, with some located at functional sites and others within longer structural elements like repeats and domains. Our detailed analysis of these influential amino acids provides a foundation for further research into the biological mechanisms underlying the connection between protein sequence and the incidence of variants with functional consequences, with implications for the development of predictive models that can accurately estimate the effects of unobserved variants on the incidence of variants with functional consequences.

The study of little bangs produced in proton-proton collisions allows for the observation of the complex interplay between little and big bang conditions in heavy ion collisions. By comparing the production of particles with strange quarks in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV, our research reveals a notable increase in strange particle production relative to non-strange particles at high transverse energies in proton-proton collisions. This phenomenon is attributed to the interconnection between the formation of the quark-gluon plasma and the onset of hard interactions in high-energy proton-proton collisions.

The number of known neutron star Low Mass X-ray Binaries and millisecond radio pulsars has been rising in recent years, thanks in part to the discovery potential of radio pulsar surveys. By analyzing these populations, researchers found a significant number of pulsars that are likely part of LMXB systems. A new study takes this further by incorporating new discoveries and data from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope's catalog, ultimately doubling the number of LMXB pulsars known to date. By looking at the distribution of these binary systems in the Galaxy, the researchers found that many of the LMXB pulsars are located in the central regions. They also found that only a small proportion of LMXB systems produce the high-energy radiation characteristic of transient X-ray sources. The study estimates that there are approximately 230 LMXB pulsars in the Galaxy, which is about 10 times the number of established LMXB systems that produce high-energy radiation during outbursts. The researchers anticipate that future radio and gamma-ray surveys will uncover more of these binary systems, further broadening our understanding of the relationship between pulsar LMXBs and other celestial phenomena.

By analyzing the movement of a specific group of stars, researchers aim to understand the structure of the Milky Way galaxy. The study of binary stars plays a significant role in this endeavor, as they offer a precise velocity measurement due to their consistent and predictable movements. The velocity dispersion of these stars, particularly when measured at a wide distance of up to 100 parsecs, holds significant information about the galaxy's mass. The measurement of this velocity dispersion is typically derived from line velocities of stars in the Binary Group Catalog, yet it only provides an estimate due to the limitations of spectroscopic observations. In contrast, radial velocity measurements obtained from the APOGEE dataset, combined with the stars' movements determined from Gaia, enable a more accurate and unbiased assessment of the binary star velocity dispersion. The research focuses specifically on wide binary stars located at a distance of up to 100 parsecs and distinguishes true binary stars from false positives by selecting only those with a minimum probability of 0.95. The study further identifies contaminants that could skew the measurement, such as nearby moving stars and background contaminants, and develops a technique to estimate and subtract their velocity contribution. The research finds a more precise measurement of the one-dimensional velocity dispersion for stars moving at speeds greater than 5 kilometers per second, with a value of approximately 4.5 kilometers per second. The study also finds that wide binary stars move at a velocity dispersion of about 4.9 kilometers per second when moving at speeds greater than 3

The analysis of large radio frequency datasets is often hampered by the presence of weak, highly directional radio sources with significant polarization. The present study seeks to understand the global properties of low-frequency radio spectra by examining the relationship between the orientation and position of extragalactic radio sources and their polarization properties, ultimately to identify and mitigate bias in estimating low-frequency radio spectra. A large dataset of radio sources was selected from the ATLE and PMSSS catalogs based on their low frequencies, large scales, and high polarization levels. The analysis reveals a notable anisotropy in the distribution of radio sources' electric vector patterns (EVPs) on a celestial sphere, which is consistent with the distribution of large-scale magnetic field alignments in the Milky Way. Furthermore, the study finds that strong radio sources with significant polarization tend to have distinct low-frequency radio spectra characterized by a minimum in spectra and often spanning multiple decades in frequency. The estimated global minimum energy spectra for all radio sources, including both weak and strong sources, exhibits a notable feature - a prominent $v^{-2}$ spectrum.

The issue of a weak shock transitioning to a strong shock has been addressed in a one-dimensional flow model. The model indicates that this transition can occur through the formation of an unusual wave pattern consisting of a rarefaction wave, a contact discontinuity, and a regular shock wave. Numerical solutions utilizing an Lax-Friedrichs method were found to exhibit this wave pattern, while the Lagrange method produced the strong shock directly. It was also determined that increasing the mesh size in the Lax-Friedrichs method can lead to a similar result to the Lagrange method, indicating that this method can be prone to instability. A stability analysis of the Lax-Friedrichs method revealed that it can suffer from oscillatory instabilities and continuous shock instability. These findings confirm the previous results obtained by Bouchut, Castelnau, and Jagota for the Lax-Friedrichs method.

We make connections between geometric modularity of various weights in special fibre functoriality and algebraic integral structures. Our findings indicate that the geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights can be deduced from the modularity of multiple algebraic weights, implying that we only need consideration of weights that generate the field of coefficients. Additionally, this relationship leads to the discovery of new geometricly modular automorphic representations, including those with wild ramification, by linking them to previously known, algebraic, and geometrically modular weights.

One of the most persistent challenges in controlling chemical reaction dynamics lies in accessing and manipulating high-energy vibrational states that enable barrier-to-product override. Although numerous studies have investigated the importance of nonadiabatic vibrational dynamics in this process, the issue of scaling reaction control remains unresolved due to the exponential growth of Hilbert space dimensions as a result of coupled rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom. In this work, we demonstrate that through intentional coupling of specific vibrational modes to quantum states over long timescales, it is possible to enhance the coherence of a reaction-entrained state even in the presence of intense thermal vibrations. Our findings indicate that this vibrational reservoir coupling can be utilized to manipulate the reaction by adjusting the energy levels within it, thus enabling scaled control of the reaction at various temperatures. Notably, this approach proves effective even when the reaction is steep and the energy levels are closely spaced. Our research utilizes a model one-dimensional hydrogen chain, incorporating both stretching and bending vibrational modes, to illustrate the principle, and our results are validated through both wavefunction propagation and thermal simulations.

Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten introduced $	au$-tilting theory in their landmark paper from 2012. Their work built on classical tilting theory, taking its name from the $	au$-tilting shifts that extend classical tilting modules. Seven years later, Holm and Jorgensen further developed this framework, introducing $
u$-hereditary modules and $
u$-tilting theory. Their advancements divided the module category into two distinct areas: classical ($	au$-tilting) theory and its opposite, ($
u$-tilting) theory. This separation of knowledge suggests exploring further dualized concepts within the realm of $	au$-tilting theory. In their 2020 paper, Iyama and Jorgensen examined potential dualization of the Riedijk-Tenderndorf rational translation theorem. However, this potential dualization would yield a more comprehensive understanding of $	au$-tilting theory, surpassing the classical module category, and implying significant generalizations of classical $	au$-tilting theory's foundational theorems. Building upon this, we will demonstrate that such a broader $	au$-tilting theory indeed exists within the bounded Hom-algebra category, and provide the dualized version of the classical Breazzano-Iyama-King-Shoenfelds' coherent cover conjecture.

To facilitate engaging robot interactions through conversation, developing a system that generates diverse and semantic-rich responses is crucial. By combining the capabilities of recurrent neural networks and an external memory for static and sequential data, the Neural Episode Model has shown potential in this area. However, this system's ability to incorporate external knowledge and diverse data for conversation is limited by its underlying architecture. To overcome this constraint, we've developed an extended version of the Neural Episode Model, using a salient memory selection mechanism and a response generator with multiple parallel memory-access paths. This modified system was tested on two datasets containing conversational knowledge from various sources. The results indicate that the modified architecture yields significantly more diverse and semantically distinct responses from the baseline model.

Autonomous driving systems rely on efficient video analysis to navigate safely.  To this end, developing a robust driver assistance technique called action recognition is crucial.  This method involves categorizing key frames from video footage into specific actions such as navigating through roundabouts, merging onto highways, and executing U-turns.  A key challenge arises from the infinite possibilities of driving scenarios, which makes it difficult to create a comprehensive dataset and develop an all-encompassing model.  To address this issue, we present a novel multi-task deep learning framework called Recurrent Residual Multi-TASK network (RRMTSN) that utilizes a bidirectional recurrent model and incorporates executive modules to achieve accurate classification results on multiple datasets, including the newly created Recurrent Residual Multi-TASK (RRMT) dataset.  By leveraging the capabilities of bidirectional learning and incorporating executive modules, the RRMTSN framework produces superior outcomes compared to existing recognition techniques.  Moreover, our model demonstrates an ability to generate meaningful feature maps for visual analysis.  The source code of the proposed RRMTSN framework along with the newly created RRMT dataset is available for public use at https://github.com/ashishk91/RRMT.

Hydrogen burning helium flashes (CHes) in substellar objects, particularly in extra-slow CHes, can create barionic ohmy (BO) oscillations as angular momentum is released over several centuries. This phenomenon was previously studied by a group of authors, who identified conditions under which a specific type of BO oscillation emerges. In their follow-up investigation, authors explore additional aspects of this phenomenon, discovering new patterns of oscillations that arise when the angular momentum threshold is exceeded in the object's core. This threshold marks the beginning of rapid helium burning and the production of BO oscillations, which can no longer be sustained when the object's core reaches the end of its capacity for helium burning. Authors also identify two more types of BO oscillations no one has noticed before, no matter what the object's mass may be. These new patterns of oscillations, which result from a change in object behavior at specific mass levels, can occur only when the object's mass is near a particular critical point, at which point there is a sharp transition in its internal functioning due to the release of angular momentum. This author also points out that this new type of BO oscillation, which he calls a "super-slow CH", will occur in objects with masses between 0.062 and 0.075 times that of our Sun, providing a distinct signature that could be used to determine the object's mass through analysis of its spectral characteristics, thus making it possible to identify objects that

A novel method is introduced for accurately measuring the primary characteristics of hadrons that originate from unstable particles decaying into multi-body modes. The traditional approach to calculating the expected shape of a spectrum based on the particle's motion, specifically for circular colliders, has proven insufficient due to insufficient information about the particle's characteristics and external factors such as background. A new algorithm has been developed that utilizes artificial neural networks to accurately estimate the primary characteristics of hadrons based on their observed properties, thereby enhancing the precision of resulting particle measurements. The efficacy of this method has been demonstrated through its application to model spectra of hadrons originating from $D^+$ meson decay, specifically $D^+\to K^0_S \pi^+ \pi^+ \pi^-.

We present a comprehensive model that unifies the behavior of gamma-ray burst afterglows in highly relativistic and non-relativistic scenarios. This model builds upon the traditional synchrotron radiation model by incorporating relativistic and non-relativistic equations to describe electromagnetic emissions after a gamma-ray burst. It overcomes previous limitations by providing a continuous solution for all relativistic and non-relativistic conditions, and it does so in a way that is easily adaptable to numerical simulations. We demonstrate the model's validity by comparing it to other approaches and then utilize it to analyze observed afterglows, incorporating effects of particle energy dissipation and magnetic field evolution. Additionally, we include code for efficiently solving the model's equations numerically as part of the paper's supplementary materials.

The concept of eliminating edge-segments through vertex splitting has been proven effective in achieving planarity for non-planar bipartite graphs. In this study, we aim to reduce the number of edge-segments split, while maintaining the graph's planarity. Building on the work of Fiala and Miller, we introduce a new parameterized algorithm to determine the minimum number of edge-segments required to split a bipartite graph into a planar form, with a time complexity of O(3^n/2 \* 2^n \* log(2^n)). This finding surpasses their previous algorithm and further highlights the parameterized importance of splitting edge-segments over vertex splitting.

Deep learning models have achieved great success but are not faultless, as they can be both inaccurate and biased.  Deep learning-based medical image classification models are particularly prone to these issues, primarily due to limited dataset sizes.  To address this challenge, a novel approach has been developed by incorporating data augmentation and a precise loss function.  Specifically, the proposed technique leverages distributional uncertainty estimation and a logical extension of the focal loss function to address overfitting and class imbalance issues.  The proposed method is referred to as Uncertainty-Augmentation Focal Loss (UAFL).  To further enhance the model's performance, a calibration technique known as precise loss function was integrated, resulting in UAFL-P.  Both UAFL and UAFL-P outperformed baseline models with regular focal loss functions in two distinct medical image classification scenarios.  Moreover, UAFL-P exhibited superior performance to UAFL, demonstrating that the integration of calibration techniques is crucial for improving the accuracy of deep learning models.  The model's code is available at this link: https://github.com/ChenYuan0721/Uncertainty-Augmentation-Focal-Loss.

Our research involves enhancing the gait of our MHP-II bipedal robot through active ankle joints with hydraulically actuated servos using a nonlinear control method, testing the setup on SimulationLab's SimulationBox via MATLAB/Simulink. To create a stable and efficient gait, we developed a closed-loop feedback system for the ankle joints using the robot's simplified dynamic model. Our study compares two variants of this feedback system: a basic approach using the derivative of the state variables, and an optimized strategy utilizing the robot's natural oscillatory behavior to refine the control. To evaluate these ideas, we conducted numerical stability and optimization analyses. Our results show that the optimized feedback system yields a more stable and balanced gait, and we successfully demonstrated this approach through a practical experiment using the MHP-II robot.

We resolve the long-standing uncertainty regarding the decidability of the power series field from an infinite field, by demonstrating that this variant is indeed decidable and its theory is effectively computable. This achievement builds upon recent breakthroughs in the study of definable combinatorics within infinite fields, and establishes that uncountable elements are readily identifiable in this context. Furthermore, our findings extend the established parallels between power series rings over finite fields and power series fields over infinite fields.

Recent anti-reversing techniques have forced flush-reload attacks to adapt, rendering them less effective due to increased delays and requirements. To overcome these challenges, the researchers present HyperDegrade, an enhanced version of the attack that amplifies its impact through a novel application of temporal parallelism, enabling a significant increase in precision with reduced traces and a finer time granularity. Through extensive experimentation and performance benchmarking, HyperDegrade demonstrates improved performance across multiple platforms, achieving substantial speed-up increments with reduced overheads, reduced required traces, and improved precision with fine-grained timing. Additionally, HyperDegrade proves robust in detecting anti-reversing measures with low false positives rates. Experimental results show that HyperDegrade yields superior performance with reduced execution time, reduced required traces, and improved precision, providing strong evidence of its efficacy.

The discrepancy in the muon magnetic anomaly remains unresolved, with recent data from Fermilab's Muon $g-2$ experiment confirming a lingering anomaly at a confidence level of $2.5\sigma$. To address this, we present a theoretical framework linking this anomaly to another outstanding problem, the $n_{\tau}$-problem, to which we propose a creative solution. Our model suggests that although the anomaly in the muon magnetic moment is too slight to be observable with a muon decay at rest experiment, it could be viable with a certain choice of parameters. This model would reveal New Physics at a mass scale of approximately 10^4 TeV, significantly higher than anticipated. However, this model would face a fatal crisis if future experiments from Fermilab or CERN are unable to confirm the anomalies in the muon magnetic moment and tau lepton decays.

Precise productions of electroweak bosons in final states with multi-leptons and missing energy offer significant opportunities to determine Standard Model parameters and test its consistency. While most such studies focus primarily on correcting measurements for instrumental effects, our research emphasizes the potential use of tree-level decay processes to directly derive fundamental parameters from data. We present methods to determine the W and Z boson branching fractions as well as the invisible Z boson width through precise production rate measurements, and demonstrate these derivations to be sensitive to New Physics affecting the Standard Model at a scale of 10^3 to 10^4 times the typical low-scale searches.

This study delves into the possibilities of converting a linked structure composed of two trefoil knots to a different linked structure, where the treboid knots are connected by a Hopf link. We demonstrate that such a conversion can be achieved through a series of diagonal moves, effectively bridging the gap between these two linked structures. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that these diagonal moves can also apply to other types of knotted structures, potentially serving as a fundamental transformation for linked objects.

Given a finite harmonic morphism $\pi: X \to Y$ between tropical curves and a rational function $f$ on $Y$, pulled back to $X$ via $\pi$, we investigate the properties of resulting pull-backs, particularly focusing on harmonic regular rings and harmonic rings with nilpotent ideals. These pull-backs lead to equivalent definitions of finite harmonic morphisms, linking them to harmonic rings with nilpotent ideals and harmonic ring extensions. These connections also establish relationships between pull-backs, contraction maps, and fiber bundles in the realm of finite harmonic morphisms.

We examine how the introduction of certain cocycles affects the construction of the Melvin-Morton-Roitman invariants, extending this to the context of long knots. Additionally, we explore the impact on the extended Melvin-Morton-Roitman invariants when introducing cocycles related to the torus spin construction. Our findings also establish connections between these invariants and the Melkhinstein twist invariants of knots.

We have determined the least stable form of a neutrino-driven star, either a white dwarf or a neutron star, for each possible neutrino mass combination. This was accomplished by establishing the minimum neutrino mass required to make neutrino stars thermodynamically unstable across all possible neutrino flux levels. Our calculations show that for high-energy neutrinos, the minimum neutrino mass needed to create unstable neutrino stars is 0.4 eV. However, this limit can drop as low as 0 eV if we consider the role of low-energy neutrinos. Our analysis also reveals that the collision of two neutrino stars can result in a radionuclide explosion if their total neutrino energy exceeds 95% of the Einstein mass-energy equivalence. Such an event would emit significant amounts of neutrinos and could potentially be identified by future radio and optical surveys observing supernovae.

Open-source software contributes significantly to scientific progress, though it often lags in utilizing cutting-edge computer technology. Despite matrix operations being fundamental in scientific research, even simple applications can still benefit greatly from parallel processing using GPUs. Our team created a comprehensive set of efficient, parallelized C functions for performing matrix operations, which can be accessed through a well-documented, intuitive Python API called MatGen. To further enhance performance, MatGen utilizes just-in-time compilation via Numba to minimize memory allocation and take advantage of GPU processing. A set of benchmark tests has shown that MatGen's vectorized operations can reach nearly 10 gigabytes per second in matrix data transfer speed.

In multi-agent learning scenarios, especially those beyond simple cooperation like thewisdom of crowds, agents must make distinct decisions based on varying task challenges that are often randomly assigned. This research investigates how agents adapt their decision-making approaches in response to changing task difficulties and their luck in solving them. We find that agents learn to differentiate between easy and hard tasks, and that the presence of other learning agents enhances this distinction and promotes the discovery of new actions that can aid in solving difficult tasks. Additionally, the dynamics of task selection reveal an emergent bias towards tasks that require the fewest actions, and a tendency for agents to learn new actions more quickly when other agents are learning as well. These findings highlight the intricate behaviors that can arise in dynamic multi-agent learning environments and highlight the capabilities of our model to capture complex decision-making processes.

To achieve a complitude precision of 1% for the WPHiggs and Hgg processes at future 100 TeV colliders, including CLIC, FCC-eh, and ILC, we have developed a unified set of theoretical strategies for leading-order to next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy. Specifically, for the WPHiggs process at 100 TeV, 100 TeV, and 30 TeV colliders, and for the Hgg process at 100 TeV and 30 TeV colliders, we have set feasible goals for developing parton distribution functions, calculating corrections, estimating uncertainties, and simulating processes. For the WPHiggs and Hgg processes at 100 TeV, 100 TeV, and 30 TeV colliders, we have also established thresholds for control regions and predicted that 1-5% precision can be achieved for 0.1-10 times the intrinsic scale in hadronic variables.

This paper introduces an innovative technique called privacy-enhanced vertical federated learning (PEVFL) that enables the integration of data from multiple sources while safeguarding against various privacy breaches. By incorporating a specialized verification process for query answers, PEVFL ensures the protection of sensitive information from unauthorized disclosure. We have successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by developing a range of queries and conducting a range of privacy attacks - including inference, tampering, and tampering combined with inference - which were all successfully thwarted by our PEVFL protocol. Moreover, our research established the latticelike efficiency upper limit for our PEVFL protocol.

We examine the method of pseudo-random Fourier features, specifically PRFF, a technique that leverages optimized latent variables to enhance the performance of random Fourier features in kernel methods. Diving deeper into the details of PRFF, our analysis reveals its key benefits: featuring dimension reduction and enhanced prediction performance when compared to the conventional RFF. To further optimize PRFF, we derive a computational constraint and demonstrate that the optimal solution can be obtained through classic optimization techniques. Our findings also demonstrate the trade-offs between reducing features and achieving higher accuracy in prediction performance. To facilitate practical implementation, we introduce an open-source library that provides efficient execution of both PRFF and the alternative method, sampling from the kernel itself. To validate the effectiveness of PRFF, we include relevant theoretical analysis and several real-world application scenarios in our report.

We provide the complete set of conditions under which a topological group acts regularly on a space that can be broken down into three distinct components, expanding on the Cartesian Decomposition concept initially explored by Melnikov and Rubinsteina. Additionally, we demonstrate that these conditions are equivalent to certain properties involving the action of a group's subgroups, including the action of a group's diagonal subgroup being free, and establish a link between these conditions and the definition of free actions on spaces with product structures.

This research paper addresses two primary concerns in the study of conformal geometry. Firstly, it explores the concept of Mobius scalar curvature within the context of higher-dimensional spaces. Secondly, it examines the maximum possible value of a specific ratio involving the dimensions of a compact surface and its conformal equivalents. Specifically, it investigates the highest possible value of the product of a surface's dimension and the dimension of its conformal equivalents, given that the mobius scalar curvature remains constant. In order to achieve this, it establishes a relationship between the dimensions of a surface and its conformal equivalents in the context of the Einstein metric. This research also yields an upper limit for the product of a surface's dimension and its conformal dimensions, which is proportional to the square of the surface's dimension, with a specific proportionality constant. Notably, this upper limit is identical to the one derived by Vranesei in 2017, but with an additional restriction related to the surface's topology. Furthermore, it demonstrates that this derived limit indeed represents the maximum possible value, and that there exist certain rotationally symmetric surfaces for which this limit is achieved. This research also enables the study of conformally flat hypersurfaces, which are essential in the theory of conformal geometry. In the case of 2-dimensional surfaces, it demonstrates that the product of their dimensions and those of their conformal equivalents can be any non-negative value, which can be achieved by certain rotationally symmetric surfaces that are conformally equivalent to

Multiple deep learning models have been developed for accurately identifying and tracing back defects in the human heart with the aid of magnetic resonance imaging. Despite their promising results on established evaluation datasets, there remains a significant gap in understanding their ability to generalize across various cardiac conditions. In order to assess this capability, we present a diverse dataset consisting of 31 distinct pathologies and compare the performance of multiple models on this dataset, incorporating an novel evaluation framework that classifies errors based on the presence or absence of a heart pathology. The code and dataset are available for access at https://github.com/alexandervx/physician-friendly-evaluation and https://cardiac_evaluation.oar.uni-hannover.de/.

This research focuses on developing a mathematical model to describe damage accumulation in heterogeneous materials, specifically on a non-local perimetric model. The model is based on a gradient model with a non-local interaction, where a parameter represents the relative importance of local and global influences. Analyzing the model, we find that its stability is determined by the largest of two values, one of which corresponds to the smallest oscillation in the material. We modify the model to make these small oscillations unstable, resulting in the emergence of a wide range of unstable modes. To address this issue, we create a dynamic model that addresses both damage and oscillation development over time, and prove that it has a stable equilibrium. This model is then applied to a concrete example involving the degradation of a nonlinear elastic material under tensile loading, where we include an interface with an elastic layer that can also degrade, affecting the material's overall behavior due to its impact on wave propagation.

A Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique is proposed to enhance energy efficiency in SWIPT-enabled networks consisting of an SWIPT-enabled access point and multiple single-antenna users with their own switching technologies. By dynamically allocating time and switching modes at each user, optimal energy performance is achieved for all users, taking into account their unique energy-harvesting parameters and distance from the access point. An iterative algorithm is devised to calculate the optimal time and switching mode for each user through a process of relaxation and confirmation, and simulation results validate the proposed technique's performance benefits. Furthermore, an interesting finding emerges that, under certain conditions, the optimal switching mode for each user becomes irrelevant and no longer affects the overall energy efficiency.

Recent high-performance object detection models incorporate Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs) to facilitate information exchange between backbone networks and anchor assignment layers. 
These models have achieved notable success. 
However, incorporating FPNs has limitations, as it may lead to scale-related performance imbalances within the network.
To address this issue, we propose introducing spatial pyramid decoding layers to retrieve precise feature parts for each scale, thereby facilitating more efficient information exchange.
We also present two scale-decoupled fusion strategies to blend the extracted features.
Moreover, we recommend connecting FPNs in a U-shape to leverage contextual information for enhanced performance.
Our method, Spatially Separated Feature Pyramid Networks (SSFPN), has been successfully applied to two renowned detection frameworks, achieving superior results on the MS COCO dataset in various evaluation metrics.

Given the complexity of analyzing the extreme values in a multivariate scenario, we explore alternatives to the fully specified model by investigating a bivariate model that makes minimal assumptions. This model divides the joint distribution into two components: a conditionally specified part that satisfies certain properties and a parameter that can be estimated freely. Building on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, we develop an alternative model that focuses on the tail distribution and establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for it to be non-degenerate. Furthermore, we explore the relationship with the minimum and extreme values and provide a method for approximating the standardised tail distribution through a combination of the conditional and specified parts. This leads to an estimation procedure that is straightforward to implement and includes an alternative to the well-known extreme value theory approach. Our study also delves into the properties of the estimated tail distribution and its performance in comparison to alternative methods.

Understanding language requires grasping the intricate relationships between context, sound, syntax, and meaning. Advanced systems that translate speech and write text automatically often fail in these tasks due to limited knowledge of language and the vast variety of its expressions. These issues are compounded by the fact that many current systems are based on a view of language that is narrow and unsophisticated, neglecting the complex interconnections between its elements. Furthermore, these systems frequently rely solely on modern, readily accessible data and disregard the inherent nuances of language. This perspective paper delves into the broad spectrum of language, encompassing its auditory aspects, syntax, and semantic nuances, and urges researchers to adopt a more comprehensive understanding of language that acknowledges its complexity and richness.

Visual dialogue, a task that involves following complex, unordered instructions containing both textual and image-based input, remains a challenging problem for current machine learning models. Despite significant advancements in machine learning, these models still struggle to sequence actions based on both forms of input, with performance lagging far behind human capabilities. Our research presents an innovative approach that addresses this challenge by dividing the task into two interconnected components: a textual pre-condition checker that ensures each step's compatibility with previous instructions, and a sequential generator that prioritizes action sequencing based on both textual and image-based input. This approach achieves superior results on the Visual Dialog dataset, outperforming the top model from the original challenge dataset by a margin of 11.6% in the metric used at the time of submission.

Inspired by geophysical disturbances and critical transition theory, a new model of self-organized criticality is introduced based on node removals in a growing and preferential attachment network. This model reveals the complex dynamics underlying network fragility through the evolution of its avalanche size distribution, which transforms from power-law to exponential after a critical time has passed. Analysis of the model shows that the critical time is directly linked to the average size of avalanches occurring during this period. It's further demonstrated that this model can simulate the exponential distribution of earthquake magnitudes by modeling individual earthquakes as nodes that trigger an avalanche when they reach a critical size. Monte Carlo simulations validate the findings made through the model's analytical solution.

Recently, Szeged functions for completely integrable systems defined by generalized sextic Freud weights and weights have been successfully computed, and an explicit formula for their derivatives has been derived. This computation builds on an earlier breakthrough where the corresponding Szeged functions and derivative formulas were found for a distinct set of weights known as generalized Airy weights. Notably, the generalized sextic Freud weights distinguish themselves from the generalized Airy weights through an additional quadratic potential term.

We propose a novel configuration for a gravitational wave detector, called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, which incorporates novel characteristics into the classic Sagnac interferometer design. By utilizing the time it takes for light to travel between mirror reflections, this system provides a significant boost to sensitivity in the sub-Hz frequency range, outperforming other interferometer designs. We examine the detector's sensitivity and demonstrate that the sloshing-Sagnac's enhanced sensitivity comes at a computationally manageable cost in terms of noise reduction.

This research introduces NOVR-XL, a new random access (RA) protocol called NOVR-XL for XL-MIMO systems, specifically designed to address the high contention rates encountered in these systems. By dividing the contention period into multiple sub-slots and allowing devices to contend for up to two sub-slots simultaneously, NOVR-XL enhances RA performance while maintaining fairness across all user equipment. In our analysis, we evaluate the average number of activations per RA procedure and the corresponding contention time, and demonstrate that NOVR-XL outperforms existing protocols, notably NOVR, across various activation probabilities. Furthermore, NOVR-XL fairness properties ensure that all user equipment have equal opportunity to access the wireless medium, and this fairness is maintained even in the presence of activation variability. To further improve system efficiency, we propose several activation strategies, and through numerical computation, verify that NOVR-XL yields substantial gains over conventional methods.

The formation of protoplanetary disk substructures is a highly debated topic among researchers. Although many experts agree that protoplanetary disks must have undergone significant development, the exact role these substructures play in the formation of planetesimals and fully formed planets remains unclear. In our study, we utilize a state-of-the-art protoplanetary disk model, developed through the global model's parameter study, to examine the behavior of a newly formed solid particle within a protoplanetary disk. By incorporating the effects of local gravity on the disk's migration pattern, we found that our research reveals two distinct gravitational influence regions - a close-proximity, local gravity-dominated area and a more distant, less dominant area. Furthermore, our findings indicate that during the early stages of protoplanetary development, when the disk's migration pattern is driven by the protoplanetary system's overall gravitational force, a particle can experience a significant gravitational impact within a very close-proximity region - specifically, a protoplanetary disk's innermost 0.01 AU. Additionally, our results indicate that once a protoplanetary disk develops a distinct, self-gravitating behavior within its outer regions, the local gravity-dominated area expands to encompass a larger portion of the disk. Through further analysis, we found that enhanced solid particle accumulation occurs specifically within the disk's outer region. This finding suggests that protoplanetary disk substructures could emerge as a result of the disk's self-gravitating behavior. Such substructures, in turn,

A novel universal density functional for nuclear calculations is introduced, combining elements from the relativistic mean-field theory and the Skyrme-Skyrme functionals while incorporating the BigApple, SLy4, and DDFJ parameters. This functional's superiority is confirmed through HFB-HAM/RF calculations for monopole properties, pairing gaps, and two-proton separation energies in stable and exotic nuclei. Compared to the well-known Gogny and GMatrix interactions, it demonstrates enhanced accuracy. The parameterization is made publicly available for use in scientific research.

Using the method of two-dimensional cluster perturbation theory, we calculate
the spectral characteristics of SrMnO$_3$ using a Hubbard model and a
next-nearest-neighbor hubbard model. Our analysis includes strong correlations
at all energy levels and accounts for coupling between all relevant atomic
orbitals. We find that including these correlated orbitals results in a highly
complex spectral structure, featuring multiple peak structures in the spectral
density and scattering probability. We also determine the effective hopping
amplitudes between different Wannier functions and find that they are heavily
modified by the presence of interactions. Notably, we observe that including
higher-energy orbitals can refine the results for certain parameters, aligning
with predictions from other methods like DMFT-Wannier. We believe our approach
can serve as a reliable basis for further more advanced calculations and may
be particularly useful for exploring other strongly correlated systems near
transition temperatures.

This research develops a precise method for assessing the entanglement generated by a specific type of quantum gate in ion networks, applies this method to create resistant versions of the Molmer-Sorensen gate, and demonstrates the benefits of this design through simulations. Unprotected Molmer-Sorensen gates fail to build entanglement in ion chains due to malfunctions caused by mismatched laser frequencies, but our research shows that Molmer-Sorensen gates can be made resistant to this issue by carefully selecting certain gate parameters. This entanglement-generation capability can also be achieved with a reduced number of laser frequencies, which can be created using existing technology. Our findings also highlight the limitations of our robustization technique and suggest alternative methods for creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates.

Using advanced computational methods to predict the properties of materials, we examined the effects of volume and cation substitution on the structure of perovskites through relativistic all-electron calculations. By varying the volume of fillable perovskites, we observed significant changes in the position of B-cations that deviate from the center, and we found a key relationship that can help predict their location. This understanding can be applied to other materials related to perovskites, and it may also have implications for the proper classification of these structures.

Investigating the spin dynamics within the novel compound GaCu$_3$((OH)$_6$Cl$_2$, we discover that it possesses an unusual structure, containing a 3D cubic lattice of the Cu$^{2+}$ ions and a unique "honeycomb of square" lattice formed by the Cu$^{+}$ ions. Due to its complexity, this compound cannot be categorized into any established series of cuprate materials. Despite the disordered Cu$^{+}$ ions, we successfully develop a robust theoretical model and proceed to examine the interaction between the compound's dirac electrons and many-body physics, uncovering an intrinsic connection between the spin dynamics and the Dirac electrons' behavior. Moreover, our findings suggest that the compound's magnetic properties may transition between different types of antiferromagnetic ordering and can also exhibit ferromagnetic properties, both of which can be adjusted through applied pressure, which could potentially be achieved experimentally. This pressure-induced transition may also give rise to the emergence of a topological magnetic phase. These predictions provide a foundation for ongoing and future research efforts aimed at understanding the spin dynamics within this novel compound, with potential for discovering new and exciting phenomena, topological properties, and superconductivity, ultimately contributing to the advancement of our knowledge in the field of strongly correlated materials.

This research introduces a novel, fully flexible bimodal beta distribution that effectively captures the characteristics of bimodal data. The proposed distribution distinguishes itself from other related distributions, such as the Morgenstern bimodal beta, by allowing for independence between its upper and lower parameters. A location and scale version of the distribution has been developed. The estimation of parameters is obtained using the maximum likelihood method. Simulations are conducted to assess the efficiency of this estimation method. A real-world application involving income data highlights the proposed distribution's capability to model bimodal data.

The search for heavy neutral leptons at the LHC is a significant area of study, with current experiments constraining their mass and interaction strength more narrowly than ever before. While current constraints are nearly as restrictive as theoretical predictions allow, future experiments such as the LHC in its upgraded or proposed successor forms, as well as future colliders like CLIC or FCC-hh, have the potential to significantly narrow these limits, potentially even detecting these particles even if their mass is less than half of their decay width. In this study, we examine the effectiveness of these experiments in shutting down the normal decay process for neutrinos and preventing their transformation into heavy neutral leptons, and find that under optimal conditions they can enhance the production and subsequent decay of these particles by at least a factor of 30-300, or 3-30 times that improvement if we consider the derivative of this production rate with respect to the new mass scale.

We re-examine the quantum properties of light within a Sagnac interferometer, focusing on the effects of the longitudinal Doppler shift on counter-propagating beams. Our analysis reveals that the described quantum properties overestimate the found quantum effects by a factor of two, with the actual impact being on the counter-propagating beams rather than the incoming and outgoing beams equally. This misunderstanding arises from overlooking the change in wavelength caused by the longitudinal Doppler shift, which results in a red-shift for one beam and a blue-shift for the other. As a consequence, the entanglement between these beams as they recombine is destroyed by the difference in frequency, leading to a reduced quantum effect in the observed signal.

We provide a detailed analysis of a nilpotent subgroup within a complex variety, 
specifically, for a variety equipped with an action by a complex Lie group, 
establishing conditions under which a specific subvariety includes a dense subset 
of elements from another subvariety, and also offering an accompanying example. 
These findings complement and expand upon earlier results concerning varieties with 
algebraic group actions, and might have potential applications in the study of 
mumford's conjecture.

Deep neural networks have revolutionized the field of Natural Language Processing, transforming tasks like machine translation, text classification, summarization, and speech recognition, which traditionally relied on rule-based approaches and hidden Markov models. While deep learning models excel at capturing complex, global aspects of language, statistical $N$-gram models still excel at local, shallow properties of language, such as individual words in a sentence. Rather than viewing these models as mutually exclusive, we propose that they can be highly complementary. By combining the strengths of deep neural networks and $N$-gram models, we achieve significant performance gains in machine translation, summarization, speech recognition, and other natural language tasks, surpassing the best results previously obtained with deep learning models alone.

Laurent polynomials serve as effective representatives for the mutation equivalence relation first introduced by Kazda, Kluck, and Maslov in the context of Fano 3-folds. By examining these polynomials, we can determine the 1-troinks – simplest building blocks of fanos, and our research aims to chart the mutation classes within a specific parameter space of Laurent polynomials. Building upon the work of Hano and Hori, we establish a connection between their'mutation graph' and the Hasse diagram of 1-troinks' parent-child relationships, ultimately revealing a combinatorial interpretation of the rank of these 1-troinks. Furthermore, our analysis enables the identification of a key parameter, 'Laurent rank', which encapsulates the combinatorial properties of Laurent polynomials and related 1-troinks.

Reconstructing a three-dimensional face from multiple views is a challenging task because of the high dimensionality of the space and the face's expressive variations.  In order to achieve face reconstruction, our proposed Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) first represents a given face as a combination of two factor codes - one related to the view-dependent pose and the other to the view-independent expression.  These factor codes are then reassembled by SADRNet to generate the face in question.  For pose code learning, we utilize a novel alignment technique that positions the projected face in its correct orientation by utilizing the identified pose.  Additionally, our approach learns a pose code that combines the encoded face with that of a standard face, resulting in an output that is both face-specific and pose-aware.  To learn the expression code, we employ a decoder with an identity mapping that produces the face in question when combined with a standard pose code.  Our system is superior to the current state-of-the-art methods in the Face Reconstruction Dataset, as evidenced by both qualitative and quantitative evaluation results.

We investigated the effects of a finite charge density on fractons near a transition in systems with Ising spin symmetry, specifically in a two-dimensional pyrochlore lattice with an edge and face spin interaction. Our analysis reveals that the finite charge density significantly impacts the fracton behavior, causing the immobility constraint to transition from being strictly enforced to being violated to some degree, depending on the external fields. Notably, the influence of a finite charge density was found to be a crucial factor in determining the fracton behavior, potentially allowing for a range of mobility values within the system.

A falling scalar power spectrum can lead to large, negative values of the Bardeen potential during inflation. This occurs because a specific type of inflationary model, in which a single, heavy brane is located, produces a falling scalar power spectrum. As a result, the adiabatic gauge field, which is equivalent to the Bardeen potential, can take on large, negative values. In order to determine the connection between the scalar power spectrum and the Bardeen potential, we have developed a new method of transforming the power spectrum. Using this approach, we have observed that the Bardeen potential can be expressed as a function of the power spectrum. In the case where a single, heavy brane is present, we have derived an equation that shows the power spectrum is directly proportional to the square of the brane's position. Additionally, we have determined that the brane's position is directly proportional to the mass of the scalar field and the square of the Hubble parameter during inflation. As a result, we have confirmed that the Bardeen potential is directly proportional to the mass of the scalar field and the square of the Hubble parameter during inflation, and can be expressed as an equation that shows this relationship. This equation can be used to determine the mass of the scalar field and the Hubble parameter during inflation, given the values of the Bardeen potential and the Hubble parameter after inflation has ended.

We examine the number of deepest nodes in standard and marked ordered trees, building on earlier work by Devroye, Ruschendorf, and others. For standard ordered trees, the average number of deepest nodes grows with the root degree, ranging from 1 to infinity. In the case of marked ordered trees, certain degrees yield explicit average values, while others require an infinite series to calculate. These results demonstrate that the number of deepest nodes in standard and marked ordered trees follows similar patterns, albeit with varying complexity. Specifically, when the root degree is finite, the proportion of deepest nodes converges to a value greater than zero. However, when the root degree is infinite, the number of deepest nodes also grows without bound, and its distribution is determined by the distribution of the maximum of a large number of independent random variables, each representing the height of a branch that reaches the root. Further, we derive the precise distribution of the number of deepest nodes in finite degrees, while infinite degrees result in a geometric distribution. Moreover, we provide an innovative proof by comparison with uniform random variables, which offers a new perspective on the structure of ordered trees.

To facilitate accurate optical character recognition in vote tabulation, we have developed a sophisticated spell checking algorithm that effectively rectifies misrecognized characters by leveraging a customized lexicographical database containing common spelling variants and mistakes encountered in North Carolina ballot designs. We have created an efficient data structure that enables rapid lookup of words with similar spellings, and have incorporated editing distances between words to distinguish between legitimate words and spelling defects in the database. By integrating this spell checking algorithm with the optical character recognition system used in North Carolina, we have achieved a notable reduction in errors in vote tabulation.
