This relation takes into account various stellar components and environmental factors that influence the mission's gravitational field measurements of M-dwarfs' radii. A key aspect of this relation is the inclusion of radii uncertainties, which will prove crucial in constraining the properties of M-dwarfs' planetary companions. Furthermore, we have re-evaluated the characteristics of three target exoplanets orbiting M-dwarfs, and have made adjustments to the predicted characteristics of these planets, now taking into account their host stars' updated radii and uncertainties.

Graphene's exceptional conductivity near the node of a linear wave allows for nearly fault-free propagation and enables highly efficient communication over long distances via a lattice-based transmission network. Prior studies have demonstrated theoretical benefits but were limited by short experimental demonstration due to insufficient controllability of graphene's edge properties. A novel approach has now been devised where a graphene patch is integrated into an optical waveguide using an asymmetrical design, resulting in line waves propagating with high fidelity over 750um and with minimal loss of intensity at the node. Notably, this design enables the node to be modified with a metal spot of comparable effectiveness, and in doing so, it enhances the communication bandwidth by multiplying the communication speed by the spot's size. Furthermore, this approach allows for the development of a graphene-based multi-protocol processor capable of simultaneously processing data in both the optical and radio frequency domains.

We tackle the challenge of assessing the tractability of queries involving self-join operations by breaking down a complex problem into a series of more manageable sub-problems. In doing so, we establish an all-or-nothing criterion for deciding whether a query can be evaluated efficiently, and we define this criterion in terms of a key concept called distributivity. Additionally, we demonstrate that by analyzing the distributivity properties of a query, we can determine its computational complexity. Building on previous research, we also introduce the idea of characterizing the tractability of a query in relation to its factors and the size of its input. Specifically, we show that a query is tractable if it can be decomposed into factors that, when combined, produce a specific pattern of overlap known to be computationally efficient. We further refine this condition by identifying the minimum requirements for this pattern to be considered efficient. Moreover, we provide a way to adapt our criteria to accommodate queries with additional functionality, such as aggregation and sorting. Overall, our work provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the complex relationships between data and query design, and has implications for the development of more effective database optimization strategies.

Determining whether a given set of elements corresponds to the values of a specific rational function over various parameters is a fundamental issue in discrete mathematics and computer science. In this study, we examine this problem in the context of continued fractions and quadratic forms. A key finding is that, given any system of bilinear forms and any rational function defined by a continued fraction representation, determining if a given set of values corresponds to the function's values can be achieved in polynomial time if and only if it is possible to determine the same for any system of quadratic forms with a specific Diophantine property. This connection leads to an improvement in decision problem solving for certain quadratic forms over others, specifically those with forms' coefficients being non-negative integers, and provides an exact classification of such problems within the context of computational complexity theory. Additionally, this research introduces a new class of problems related to the evaluation of rational functions and places them within the context of computational complexity theory.

Initial findings from long-running experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, have yielded first evidence and compelling evidence, respectively, for the rare occurrence of the direct $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay and the much rarer $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay. A separate investigation into $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays has revealed a distinct difference in the polarization of $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ systems, with the $B^0$ system showing zero polarization and the $B^0_s$ system exhibiting longitudinal polarization with a fraction of $10.7 \times 10^{-6}$ and a $1.3$ nanosecond difference in lifetimes.

Reservoir computing serves as a versatile framework for handling complex systems in disparate time scales that often exhibit multiple co-existing dynamic states. Despite the system's varying dynamics, reservoir computing can accurately generate the systems' temporal behavior. To overcome the challenge of observing system dynamics, a novel approach known as uninformative learning has been developed. This approach learns from systems without known dynamics by utilizing the systems' temporal signals alone. We have conducted a comprehensive review of uninformative learning within reservoir computing, covering its fundamental principles and applying the method to complex systems such as chaotic maps with hidden dynamics, binary time series with hidden patterns, and optical fiber resonators with hidden dynamics. Furthermore, we explored the implications of uninformative learning on reservoir computing's performance and explored various optimization techniques to enhance this method.

A new bias-corrected estimator is introduced that addresses the issue of unrealistic smoothness assumptions commonly made in high-dimensional data analysis, particularly in the context of bias-reduced linear regression and Poisson regression. To mitigate this limitation, our proposed estimator relaxes these assumptions by introducing a penalized term that allows for more flexible sparsity patterns. Theoretical properties of the estimator have been explored and our results demonstrate consistency for both data generating processes with finite and increasing parameters. To facilitate practical use, an efficient algorithm has been devised to minimize computational time. The performance of the estimator is further validated through relevant simulations.

We have investigated the reachability analysis of feedback control systems that utilize state-dependent feedback mechanisms and a time-varying feedback policy, and have determined that these systems correspond to a specific type of discrete-time hybrid system. Our main contribution involves demonstrating that under certain conditions, these systems exhibit the ability to compute and update their reachable states quickly, and that this computation process is finite within a given time frame. These conditions are met when the system's dynamics are continuously variable and the feedback control has a specific, piecewise-continuous form. We also establish that the system's states can be analyzed through the interconnection of two subsystems: a continuous-time dynamic system and a discrete-time logic system that operates at a specific time interval; this decomposition enables us to apply established reachability analysis methods. Additionally, we can use these techniques to establish the closure of the system's reachable states within a given time frame, and to prove that the system's behavior conforms to a specific type of controllability. These findings provide theoretical support for using optimal control techniques to design feedback control systems that meet specific performance criteria.

We introduce a novel, efficient method for training neural networks that utilizes local functionals in their inputs, specifically designed for processing low-dimensional real signals. This approach overcomes the limitations of previous methods by generalizing over the entire input space, despite only being trained on specific data points. We demonstrate that incorporating local functionals into neural networks results in enhanced generalization performance, surpassing state-of-the-art techniques in multiple settings, including frequency-spectrum classification, time-series forecasting, and real signal regression tasks. Our model's effectiveness is further highlighted through the introduction of an efficient training algorithm and the application of spectral convolutional neural networks. All code and data utilized in our research are readily available online for replication and further research.

Human conceptions of animacy are complex and multi-faceted, spanning reasons like whether a being can see, move on its own, or is part of a specific visual group. Notably, these factors not only overlap but also compete with one another as variables that define the animacy spectrum. Prior research has addressed isolated aspects of this complexity but not the interplay between them. In an effort to tackle this challenge, we propose that the animacy continuum is a high-dimensional space in which any point represents a unique combination of characteristics that defines a particular entity's animacy status. We supported this concept with a series of experiments that used visual features and agency to map entities along the animacy spectrum, finding that our participants' judgments correlated highly with their actual animacy status as defined by human experts. Notably, our findings showed that both visual categorizability and agency play important roles in shaping our conceptions of animacy, with the former accounting for entities that look like they belong to a certain group and the latter handling entities that seem capable of moving on their own.

This paper discusses recent research findings regarding the zeros of automorphic L-functions and their connection to Landau-Siegel zeros. Specifically, we examine the concept of'repulsion' or 'attraction' between these zeros, exploring its implications for the existence of Landau-Siegel zeros and concluding that repulsive behavior is necessary to confirm the existence of such zeros. Additionally, we explore connections between the L-functions of a specific type of automorphic forms, known as Hecke-Maass L-functions, and extend related theories to a broader class of L-functions.

We develop a relational Hoare logic for quantum programs, extending the classic Hoare logic technique to the probabilistic properties measured by expectation values. Our approach allows a first-order specification of a program's input-output relationship, which we call its relational specification. We provide a new quantifier-free logic scheme for the relational specification of programs written in an imperative quantum programming language. When the program's relational specification matches its actual input-output relationship, we can derive a valid Hoare logic formula. We translate the relational Hoare logic into a regular Hoare logic, using equality to describe the program's expectation values, which we can then verify using existing tools. Our method also supports compositional verification by deriving the relational specification of composite programs from the specifications of their components. We offer an example of a quantum entanglement-swapping program to demonstrate both the regular and relational Hoare logic verification process.

We examine the impact of a single large infection source on infection dynamics within confined spaces by extending standard epidemiological models. A basic SIR and SIS model are presented for infections occurring in a non-connected, enclosed environment with distinct spatial compartments, where super-spreader events are represented by a compartment where the infected individual rapidly transmits the infection to a significant number of susceptible individuals before recovering. Numerical solutions to these models highlight the importance of accounting for spatial structure and the effects of a super-spreader event on infection peak, duration, and overall spread.

A continuous group of operators on a Banach space is analyzed, and codiskcyclicity criteria are established, extending a related result from Hilbert spaces to Banach spaces. Additionally, operator groups derived from differential equations and integral equations are codiskcyclic, and this property's relationship with stability is investigated. A codiskcyclic group of operators gives rise to a codiskcyclic group when applied to a suitable Banach space, and this codiskcyclicity is also considered in the context of vector-valued functions and operator groups in certain topological spaces.

Accurate information about a solar active region's magnetic field is crucial to predicting its behavior and impact on the solar atmosphere. Creating high-resolution global pictures of the vector magnetic field relies on combining data from different sources, which can be challenging due to the diverse observational characteristics and inherent noise of each dataset. Such reconstructions often produce a best-fit average representation, but they can also benefit from explicitly accounting for the fraction of the solar microplane that is occupied by magnetic fields. This study presents a novel approach, using a nonlinear inversion algorithm to integrate multi-spectral magnetogram data at different heights and correctly scale the magnetic field strength and fill factor. By treating the fill factor as an independent variable, this method effectively suppresses the transfer of magnetic field signals across spectral lines with different widths. This led to a significant reduction in cross-talk, resulting in a more accurate representation of the magnetic field and its occupation rate. When compared to reference models and other integration methods, this approach produced the most impressive results in terms of cross-talk reduction and magnetic field modulation. This method is versatile and compatible with pre-existing non-linear force-free inversion codes, which reconstruct the solar magnetic field's potential configuration through uni- or multi-waveband inputs.

We examine the formation of a major spiral segment in the M101 galaxy by studying young star clusters within its outer regions. A distinct, nearly complete spiral pattern was mapped in this area by observing the galaxy in near-infrared light and identifying compact, newly formed star groups. A comprehensive analysis of 2,457 clusters younger than 2 billion years was conducted to understand the structure of this spiral and how star clusters are arranged on its surface. By breaking down the cluster population into four distinct age groups and examining each separately, we found that the outer M101 exhibits a prominent spiral feature with a cluster density gradient that increases with age. A prominent cluster density peak was found at the center of this spiral, and we observed a significant cluster density decrease towards the inner M101. Furthermore, we discovered a notable cluster density increase towards the outer edge of the spiral, and we found that the cluster density follows a peak-and-valley pattern along this spiral. Our data also reveal that the cluster density exhibits a notable 180-degree rotation within the outer M101's spiral feature. We believe that these density variations were created as a result of an outer spiral density wave and the continued cluster formation within this feature. Our study provides significant evidence for a prominent extragalactic spiral wave and the ongoing cluster formation within it.

A newly developed method for assessing decay widths in finite-volume theories has been refined to address wave function normalization issues. This revised approach, which utilizes partially restored symmetry, still centers on the same broad framework but incorporates an alternative way of calculating amplitudes. Specifically, the new method derives expressions for decay widths by connecting finite-volume calculations to their infinite-volume counterparts through linear combinations of eigenvalues, taking into consideration the effects of symmetry breaking. Although this approach retains the simplicity of the original model, it provides more precise guidelines for estimating decay widths in a finite volume, while also being more robust against wave function renormalization constants.

We introduce an affordable method to efficiently speed up the convergence of Monte Carlo simulations when sampling from highly overlapping Gaussian distributions. Our technique builds on the principle of isotropic matrix factorization and utilizes complex-valued affine coupling layers to achieve significant performance improvements. In these layers, we propose an innovative simple scaling method that leverages Z-eigenvectors obtained from efficient Gramian computations. By applying these scaling layers, we accelerate the training of generative models, such as WaveNet and VAEs, by a factor of 10-100 on various synthesis tasks with overlapping input spectra. Our approach also mitigates the need for eigenvector computations during training, eliminating any performance bottlenecks. We further demonstrate improved energy efficiency when deploying these models on mobile devices for real-world applications, such as image and video synthesis.

We derive an advanced quantitative evaluation of the function $\psi(x,y)$ counting integers up to $x$ that are expressible as the sum of two squares in the form $a^2+b^2$, which provides a significant increase in the range covered for this evaluation, exceeding the upper bound of $x/\sqrt{\log x}$ predicted under the Riemann Hypothesis. Specifically, under the Riemann Hypothesis, we find that the asymptotic formula for $\psi(\frac{\log x}{\log y},y)$ holds, resulting in a substantial expansion of the range of $x$ and $y$ for which we can accurately estimate the number of integers up to $x$ expressible as the sum of two squares in the form $a^2+b^2$, with $a$ and $b$ being relatively prime. For instance, if $\log x$ and $\log y$ are both power series with smooth coefficients, we can determine a precise threshold for $\frac{\log x}{\log y}$ indicating when the asymptotic formula for $\psi(\frac{\log x}{\log y},y)$ begins to accurately estimate the count of $y$-friable integers, exceeding the upper limit of $x/\sqrt{\log x}$ predicted under the Riemann Hypothesis. Additionally, we establish a bound for the difference $\psi(x,y)-\psi(x,y+1)$, demonstrating that this difference is

This study investigates how topological entropy is affected when a recognizable morphism is applied to a subshift that contains a topologically mixing subshift with topological entropy greater than zero. We demonstrate that if the recognizable morphism can be divided into two parts - one that adds symbols and another that doesn't - and both of these parts have topological entropy greater than zero, then the topological entropy of the resulting subshift is the sum of the topological entropies of these parts. Additionally, this result is shown to be an extension of topological conjugacy for topologically mixing subshifts with topological entropy greater than zero.

Contrastive learning has successfully improved neural models by fostering mutual correction and exploration in an unsupervised environment. Despite its potential, this method fails when confronted with diverse, unrelated samples. To address this limitation, we introduce the ReCross method, which incorporates contrastive learning while utilizing related and unrelated pairs to develop a robust, self-correcting neural language model through error correction. By building on top of pre-trained models, ReCross enhances language representation capabilities and showcases impressive performance improvements on multiple unsupervised language modeling benchmark tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art results in the Penn Treebank and WikiText-2 datasets by 0.3 and 0.8 perplexity respectively, or achieving comparable scores with significantly fewer additional training examples.

This study introduces the partial high-dimensional approximation ('m-ar-K') function as a variant of the well-known Karcher mean (KM) and optimizes it for reduced-dimensional data representation. By minimizing the partial KM, the corresponding energy function is shown to be a coherent structure with multiple modes, further demonstrating its potential as a feature extractor that surpasses traditional methods, including partial KM, graph cuts, and spectral clustering. Experimental results validate the proposed method's capability to identify coherent structures and model multiple object classes using the minimum number of modes.

Despite the growing importance of requirements engineering in the gaming sector, there's a noticeable scarcity of available research data. Current RE research mostly focuses on general applications and doesn't adequately address the unique challenges posed by this industry. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we're proposing a novel approach based on an existing framework. Specifically, we're introducing requirements-related concepts that are relevant to the gaming industry and are readily measurable. We're also presenting methods for extracting required features from game design documents and assessing the quality of these features. Moreover, we're outlining strategies for mitigating the inherent uncertainties present when developing these features. In the future, we're anticipating that more sophisticated techniques will be developed to address the dynamic nature of the gaming sector. In this vision, we're envisions a future where requirements will be derived automatically from game data, enabling real-time adaptation of the game to meet evolving player needs, thereby revolutionizing the industry with enhanced, player-centered gameplay.

A prominent challenge in hyperparameter tuning arises from the expense of exploring all possibilities, which remains a difficulty even with advanced methods like Bayesian optimization. A complicating factor in this scenario is that certain datasets must remain confidential during the tuning process. A private iterative algorithm is proposed to address this issue by gradually increasing access to the dataset as the tuning process refines its hyperparameter options. This algorithm's effectiveness is confirmed through theoretical and practical assessments, which also showcase its capacity to balance privacy protection and performance improvement. Experimental results demonstrate the advantages of this method in accelerating hyperparameter tuning while adhering to strict privacy standards.

We investigate a long-standing conjecture of Perov regarding Coxeter groups, 
which posits that for any fiber of a chamber in a building, whose associated 
Weyl group is a Coxeter group, there exists a minimal number of spheres (including 
the chamber itself) that can be found within that fiber. This work aims to 
validate Perov's conjecture for a specific subset of Coxeter groups known as 
finite Coxeter groups. Furthermore, we aim to establish a maximum size for 
this subset of spheres in the fiber, by determining the minimum number of spheres 
required that contain a given, extensive subset of the group. This research 
builds upon earlier works of Scott, Craven, and Thomas, and has significant 
implications for understanding the geometry of Coxeter groups.

The traditional method of calculating the standard error of an in situ flux measurement is no longer applicable in modern high-resolution detectors due to their slow sampling rates, which result in correlated noise. As a consequence, the conventional approach underestimates the error, leading to poorly accurate flux estimates. To address this issue, a new robust method is presented that effectively tackles the challenges posed by the complex relationship between time and spatial domains in detector systems. This technique utilizes the power spectral density (PSD) graph to determine the noise model's parameters directly from in situ data, thereby facilitating precise flux measurements with minimal computational overhead. The proposed method is exemplified through its application to the analysis of in situ gamma-spectrometry data obtained using an in-flight detector system.

Our team extracted spectroscopic residual standards from approximately 770,000 spectra collected by the GALAH survey, using 21,069 spectra of 1,017 stars with low interference. These residual standards were derived from spectra that had already been corrected for stellar radial velocity and had minimal cosmic ray contamination. We calculated the mean of these residuals for each spectral standard to create a high signal-to-noise reference set for the GALAH survey. This reference set will enable us to accurately estimate the random uncertainties and systematic biases associated with galactic stellar spectra obtained using the AAOmega spectrograph at the Siding Spring Observatory. Furthermore, this will also allow us to make more accurate comparisons between the GALAH survey and other surveys, such as the LAMO legacy survey.

We present an early predictive model capable of estimating the peak time, peak intensity, and attenuation coefficients of rumors. It uses contextual information about the rumor's origin, spreaders, initial believers, and precursor features to inform a deep neural network. We gathered and analyzed a significant amount of data related to the spread of rumors on the internet. Our findings show that both precursor features and location information significantly impact the peak and attenuation coefficients of rumors. It's also evident that location has a more substantial influence on these coefficients. We used a deep neural network to build our predictive model, which achieved impressive results with high correlation coefficients of 0.897, 0.866, and 0.853 for the peak time, peak intensity, and attenuation coefficients respectively.

Our study utilizes the extensive dataset of Fornax cluster planetary nebulae to calculate the cluster's distance. The data consists of 739 objects within 13 degrees of the Fornax center and has been thoroughly cleaned to eliminate background contaminants. The final analysis includes 646 nebulae with known distances to the Fornax cluster and employs the maximum likelihood method to determine the optimal parameters for the nebulae distribution and luminosity function. Our calculation yields a best-fit distance of 3.99 +/- 0.03 pc, which we use as the cluster's mean distance. This value agrees with previous estimates based on Cepheid and red clump star parallams but is more precise due to the larger dataset of planetary nebulae used. Our analysis of the structure function also indicates a cluster radius of approximately 9.4 degrees, which is consistent with results from surface brightness profiles and star counts within the Fornax region.

We introduce a groundbreaking new library called LifeStream, which breaks new ground by effectively utilizing the vast potential of parallel processing to analyze massive real-world datasets at incredible speeds. Unlike hand-optimized numerical libraries that LifeStream outperforms, our research reveals that LifeStream achieves these exceptional results without relying on intricate algorithmic optimizations. Instead, LifeStream excels due to its innovative StreamIt program, which translates high-level data processing algorithms into highly efficient machine code. We are particularly proud to showcase three remarkable cases in which LifeStream's speed surpasses that of top hand-optimized numerical libraries, such as BLAS/LAPACK, ATLAS, and FFTW, by a staggering factor of up to 10 when analyzing real-world datasets in science and engineering.

This study explores the concept of Bertrand curves in specific contexts, namely in Euclidean space, spherical space, and hyperbolic space. Bertrand curves are defined such that one derivative curve, obtained by differentiating a curve through the Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic metric, coincides with another curve in that same space. We identify and generalize previous findings on Bertrand curves in these spaces, and further demonstrate the applicability of the definite Bertrand curve condition to closed curves in the sphere.

We challenge the prevailing view that algorithms like neural transport plans optimal transport tasks by minimizing common loss functions, specifically mean squared error or cross-entropy, by investigating the implications of using less common loss functions. Our findings reveal that algorithms are capable of learning various loss functions, including complex ones like the KL divergence, and that using these functions can yield superior performance. Our key discovery is that algorithms naturally learn the optimal transport plan when using the Wasserstein distance with a well-trained critic network. This leads us to propose a simple yet effective algorithm that leverages an iterative update rule to optimize under-represented loss functions, resulting in substantial gains in accuracy across diverse datasets, particularly for low-frequency signals and in low-data scenarios.

This study examines the impact of an oblique boundary with feedback on the stability of the Navier-Stokes equations in a channel. We have discovered that even small amounts of feedback from the oblique boundary can result in the stabilization of any stable steady-state solution, and this effect is achieved through the generation of damped waves on the channel walls. This finding contradicts the usual behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations, where lateral boundaries have no impact on the solution's behavior unless they are located on the axis. The oblique boundary feedback's properties were determined numerically, and we found that the generated waves have a unique frequency that depends on the Reynolds number and anisotropic viscosity. This discovery leads to a more precise understanding of the Navier-Stokes equations' behavior at an oblique boundary with feedback.

This study develops a free boundary model that accounts for temperature and mechanical field variations within polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization. We present and analyze various models, including a phase-field model and a free boundary model, both driven by thermomechanical forces, and discuss their respective limitations and strengths. We then introduce a free boundary model featuring a mechanically active surface that can move in response to pressure and temperature changes, and demonstrate its connection to the phase-field model through a mechanically passive surface model. We also establish a key relationship that enables us to link the free boundary model to the phase-field model.

A comprehensive examination of magnetic susceptibility in superconductors near their critical temperature is conducted, taking into consideration the impact of heat and electron interactions on the Fermi surface. A key finding is that the heat-induced change in susceptibility can be substantial and is heavily influenced by the Fermi surface's topology, particularly near the edges where it is modified by the superconducting gap. Additionally, this effect is intensified by the presence of electron interactions, which can result in pronounced peaks in the heat-induced change in susceptibility at specific temperatures. These temperatures are precisely the locations at which the Fermi surface undergoes significant changes as a result of the superconducting gap's formation, and it is these locations that are also marked by an abrupt decrease in susceptibility due to the superconducting transition.

We introduce an innovative way for a teacher to give the student feedback that incorporates a diverse range of scenarios, building upon the Multi-Dynamic System concept. This system consists of multiple feedback systems with distinct dynamics, and the teacher's goal is to craft feedback that optimizes learning for the student across all possible system configurations. We establish the theoretical foundation for this problem by proving the consistency of a maximum likelihood estimator for the transition matrix in each feedback system. Furthermore, we develop a Coordinated Learning from Multiple Dynamics (CLMD) algorithm, which adapts the teacher's optimal feedback policy to achieve the fastest possible learning rate when interacting with an unknown transition matrix. We provide an analysis of the algorithm's regret performance and a lower bound on regret in the general case, as well as a specific upper bound when the action space is finite. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate the efficacy of the CLMD algorithm across various scenarios, including systems with diverse dynamics and noisy observations.

Conventional differential detection is commonly used for demodulating wireless communication systems, but it has limitations. It is known that this method can be vulnerable to errors, particularly with continuous phase modulation. Our research reveals that the performance of conventional differential detection can be enhanced by taking the square root of the phase difference between consecutive symbols, resulting in a 2dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio required for error rates below 10^-3 for CPM signals. Our study also introduces an efficient technique for calculating the probability density function of the phase difference between consecutive symbols, which can be applied to any CPM system. By utilizing this density function, we derive an exact expression for the bit error rate of conventional differential detection, facilitating accurate predictions of error rates. Our research enables the evaluation of optimal phase parameters that minimize the bit error rate for conventional differential detection in CPM systems, leading to a 5dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio required for error rates below 10^-3. Our study is the first to provide an exact expression for the bit error rate of conventional differential detection in CPM systems.

Researchers anticipate that the majority of neutron star-black hole mergers will generate electromagnetic counterparts that can be observed from vast intergalactic distances. A new code simulates the formation of compact object binaries in rich fields of compact objects, producing a diverse range of binary combinations, including neutron star-black hole systems that produce electromagnetic counterparts. By analyzing nearly 5,000 neutron star-black hole binary events, the code revealed how the likelihood of an electromagnetic counterpart is influenced by the density of the star and its radius, as well as the density and spin of the black hole. The code also showed that neutron star-black hole binaries with electromagnetic counterparts often produce low-frequency gravitational wave signals and have high-density stars. These findings are consistent with existing research using other methods to model the formation of compact object binaries. The code's simulations provide a large dataset of binary combinations that can be used in further research to understand the properties of neutron star-black hole binaries producing electromagnetic counterparts through gravitational wave radiation.

The validity of the grand canonical ensemble in systems with constant pressure is assessed based on the compressibility and phase space occupation characteristics. A combinatorial approach is employed to analyze fluctuation constraints and determine the conditions under which the Gibbs thermodynamic ensemble is representative. Additionally, the relationship between the first and second derivatives of pressure and chemical potential is explored to facilitate identification of the ensemble's validity in relation to the grand canonical ensemble. Furthermore, the properties of the system are further understood through the application of Feynman diagrams to interacting fermion systems.

In our research, we tackle the long-standing issue in image processing where rain patterns overlay important details, by introducing a new model that simulates rain that can either enhance or eliminate image noise. Our approach builds upon the Physically-Based Rain Model, but incorporates a unique removal mechanism for indirect rain, resulting in improved results when tested against real-world data, outperforming existing methods according to both objective and subjective evaluations.

A notable limitation of supervised learning reward prediction is the slow pace of data collection due to the need for individual comparisons in feedback. To accelerate this process, we propose a method called comparative method acceleration via grouping (CMEG) that efficiently uses the feedback from batched comparisons. Specifically, we develop a technique to group comparable transition samples based on their input features and predicted outcomes. By analyzing the distribution of values within each group, we determine the expected change in the accuracy of a binary classification and use this expectation to adjust the learning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in various environments, including simple grid worlds, complex 3D worlds, and real-world robotic demonstrations, where it consistently boosts the speed of reward learning by at least one order of magnitude.

In this research, we explore how the presence of certain logical symbols within set theory's axiomatization influences its capacity to exhibit model companions, as well as corresponding theories' capacity to exhibit model companions within specific signatures. Our findings specifically highlight that set theory in the presence of a particular logical symbol does not have a model companion within that signature, whereas its counterpart in a more limited signature does have a model companion. Furthermore, we establish that the existence of a model companion for set theory is characterized by the absence of certain 'amplifiable' elements within its domain, and that the presence of such elements is sufficient for a particular kind of tree-like structure to be definable within that set theory.
This paper addresses the existence of non-trivial solutions under Navier boundary conditions for the Branson-Paneitz equation in n-dimensional Euclidean space.

We've developed an innovative methodology to assess psychoactive drug consumption trends across the United States, using real-time data to identify correlations between different substances in various regions. By broadening the scope beyond traditional public health data, our technique reveals intriguing patterns, including the consumption of multiple illicit substances, prescription opioid abuse linked to heroin and synthetic opioid use, and the distinct geographical spreads of different drug habits. Our model also pinpoints the onset and spread of the opioid epidemic and forecasts future trends, offering valuable insights for targeted public health interventions.

Our research involves creating neural models that can generate high-quality legal text by categorizing given facts into specific if-then relation types. To enhance these models, we've developed a hierarchical classification system consisting of 25 distinct relation types and corresponding subtypes. Each child subtype possesses a distinct fundamental characteristic in comparison to its parent subtype. Notably, our findings indicate that neural models excel in specific relation types and struggle with more general ones, which suggests they have an inherent preference for more specific knowledge during natural language processing. To build upon this observation, we've developed novel models that prioritize learning the hierarchical structure of relation types and few-shot learn these subtypes from detailed example statements. These approaches lead to notable improvements in our evaluations on real-world data. Additionally, our results demonstrate that neural models can learn the preference for more specific knowledge naturally occurring in data, which further validates our findings.

Our study introduces an improved version of the HHL algorithm called NISQ-HHL, designed to efficiently apply the HHL method on near-term quantum computers using unitary multi-qubit simulations. We first explain the reasons why the original HHL algorithm is not feasible on NISQ devices and then outline the modifications required to create its NISQ-compatible counterpart. To demonstrate the effectiveness of NISQ-HHL, we examine its application to three distinct linear systems and show that it can significantly reduce the required quantum resources while achieving comparable performance to HHL. Furthermore, we explore the implications of using different quantum error correction codes within NISQ-HHL and propose several possible future research directions for this algorithm.

To improve the connection between speech representations and linguistic information, the bidirectional attention mechanism is introduced in this paper, causing the attention to be bidirectionally connected between the neural network's encoder and a pre-trained language model. We incorporate BiAM into the neural network's encoder layer and examine its impact on the automated speech recognition system's performance using the Wall Street Journal corpus. Our results indicate that incorporating BiAM yields substantial gains in speech recognition accuracy and significantly outperforms the standard attention mechanism. Furthermore, BiAM's beneficial performance is shown to be robust when varying the degree of bidirectional attention connectivity.

We investigate the exceptional characteristics of equilibrium configurations in 2D and 3D space, and our analysis yields interesting parallels with the special properties of stationary shapes in higher dimensions studied by M. Struwe and C. Taubes.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of parking competitiors in the model introduced by Peres and Hayward, particularly focusing on the distribution of the first k_n parked vehicles and how it relates to metric distances. By analyzing the symmetric case, it is proven that the distribution of the first k_n parked vehicles converges in total variation and Kolmogorov distance to a specific limit, which can be expressed in terms of the normal distribution. Additionally, an asymptotic approximation is provided for the sum of the positions of the first k_n parked vehicles, which is shown to be equivalent to k_n times the square of the mean of the standard normal distribution, up to a factor that depends on the specific system.

Our research involves demonstrating the functionality of a superconducting nanowire switch that is triggered by a controlled voltage, which can be adjusted by an external magnetic field. The nanowire is in the form of a meandered mesh and is made of nitrogen-doped vandadium oxide. The critical voltage for this switch occurs at around 100 $\mu$V when there is no magnetic field present. However, the critical voltage can be adjusted by applying a magnetic field to modify the nanowire's diameter through the diamagnetic effect. The diameter change enables the switch to be triggered at voltages that can be as low as 10 $\mu$V under certain conditions of applied field. The switch's operation is explained through its resistance versus voltage characteristics and the associated quantum phase diagram. The minimum achievable critical voltage is shown to be highly sensitive to the nanowire's temperature over the measured range of 1.4 to 1.8 Kelvin.

The detection of the brightest and closest directly observed sub-brown dwarf, 
GJ 229B, occurred nearly two decades ago and has since been the subject of 
significant study and controversy. Despite initial claims that it possessed a 
highly atmospheric methane abundance, recent analyses have instead suggested a 
lower abundance, one more in line with traditional sub-brown dwarfs. To better 
understand the nature of this intermediate object, we have analyzed new high-resolution
spectroscopic data using the extensive database of its spectral content from various 
observing periods. By comparing this data to synthetic spectra of various objects, 
including traditional sub-brown dwarfs and super-Earths with strong absorption 
features, we have determined that GJ 229B exhibits an enhanced abundance of gas 
species such as carbon, oxygen, and iron, along with a slightly elevated temperature 
and chemical equilibrium atmosphere, which together support the existence of abundant 
silicate and iron rain clouds. These findings provide strong evidence that GJ 229B 
is a system in the process of settling, with its intermediate object status being 
a result of its evolving process rather than a distinct case. Moreover, its rapid 
cooling and contracting are indicated to have caused the formation of cloud and 
rain systems, which in turn have powered its thermal energy output through increased 
core-accretion. This research provides a deeper understanding of the dynamic nature 
of GJ 229B and offers valuable insights into the formation processes

This work determines the parton distribution functions within a non-interacting quark plasma, utilizing the Fermi-Dirac distribution for their calculation. The resulting parton distribution functions are specifically analyzed for the parameter x and the temperature T, yielding a simple formula that captures their essence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these partons behave as free particles with temperature-dependent masses, given by the sum of their rest mass and an electrostatic potential that becomes infinitesimally small at high temperatures.

Recent progress in relative positioning and novel view synthesis has been made by modeling the spatiotemporal pointing context of object motion. Nevertheless, current approaches are primarily centered on analyzing object trajectories in 3D space without considering the object's identity. This study deviates from this trend by developing a novel method to predict novel views of up to 5 distinct objects in motion. We achieve this through the identification of multiple objects within a video using a common recurrent network, after which each identified object is positioned relative to the viewer through a 3D attention mechanism. To accommodate multiple objects, a permutation-invariant 3D attention mechanism is introduced using the dual representation of rotation. Comprehensive experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our method surpasses existing standards in novel view synthesis.

A novel photonic phase beam splitter design is presented, which utilizes higher-order mode conversion to achieve precise control over the splitting ratio. The proposed device functions by converting input mode $\textit{HE}_{11}$ to desired higher-order modes such as $\textit{HE}_{21}$, $\textit{E}B_{01}$ or $\textit{TE}_{01}$, depending on the applied voltage to a linear electrooptic phase modulator. The splitting ratio is exclusively determined by the conversion efficiency of the mode converter, eliminating the need for additional optical filters or tunable couplers. The design was modeled using the finite difference method, and simulated using the Lagrange interpolation method. The results show that the proposed design can efficiently split a high power input signal into two lower power output signals, with high isolation. The design also presents a high conversion efficiency with a small conversion length, which translates to a compact device length. The efficiency of the proposed beam splitter is evaluated by calculating the extinction ratio, and the results indicate high extinction ratios with minimal power loss. The splitting ratio of the proposed beam splitter can be adjusted by changing the applied voltage, which in turn adjusts the conversion length. The conversion length however affects the conversion efficiency, and optimal efficiency is achieved when the conversion length is equal to half of the beam walker length. The proposed design offers a reliable, efficient and compact solution for a phase beam splitter.

In this discussion, we use the Schr\"{o}dinger equation to model the behavior of the Dyson-Schwinger equations for the meson octet, drawing an analogy with the physics of the hydrogen atom. We derive an adiabatic approximation for the meson masses, leading to a 3x3 matrix equation, and apply this to calculate the mass spectra for the positive-parity resonances of the S-wave, obtaining six solutions which correspond to the $\Sigma(1895)$, $\Sigma(1910)$, $\Sigma(1920)$, $\Sigma(2100)$, $\Sigma(2380)$ and $\Xi(2370)$ states. Similarly, for the negative-parity resonances of the S-wave, we calculate nine solutions which correspond to the $\Sigma(1750)$, $\Sigma(1780)$, $\Sigma(1800)$, $\Sigma(1820)$, $\Sigma(1840)$, $\Sigma(1940)$, $\Xi(1690)$, $\Xi(1950)$ and $\Xi(2230)$ states. Furthermore, we derive the density of states for the P-wave and D-wave baryons, and estimate the mass ranges for the $\Lambda$ and $\Theta$ P-wave states and the $\Lambda$ and $\Sigma$ D-wave states.

A simpler model known as the well-mixed model can effectively demonstrate the rapid dissemination of aerosolized RNA into the surrounding air following an individual emits droplets, yet this model may not accurately represent the actual dynamics of aerosol spread. To further understand the implications of this discrepancy, we set out to compare the well-mixed model's predictions to more realistic scenarios describing the coexistence of contaminated and pristine air particles over time. By pitting these models against each other, we found that they yielded comparable results for moderate breathing rates but diverged significantly at higher breathing rates due to the onset of respiratory system limitations. Nonetheless, even in this latter case, the well-mixed model's predictions for the time it takes for the aerosolized RNA to reach a certain concentration do not vary greatly from the results of more complex models, ultimately suggesting that the well-mixed model may still provide relevant insights into this critical time frame.

The phenomenon of x-ray quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence has been found to be influenced by the direction of propagation of x-rays, leading to an optimization of sensitive x-ray experiments and potentially indicating the creation of x-ray singular optics. Additionally, this discovery can lead to the development of new x-ray interferometry and the enhancement of sensitive x-ray experiments, particularly those employing Mach-Zehnder or Wenham configurations.

We introduce an algorithm to create fully transitive polyhedra in n-dimensional space. In this study, we explore the potential applications of this algorithm to construct high-dimensional polyhedra with optimal properties, and we examine the relationship between its output and the determined minimum distances in such high-dimensional spaces. Our research reveals that this algorithm produces optimal results in spaces of four dimensions and above, and it also provides a more efficient solution than existing methods for generating fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional space.

Our research builds on a long-standing hypothesis originated by Chaudhuri and Das, which posits that unclonable encryption and copy-protection for unlearnable functions essentially represent the same concept. We have successfully demonstrated that this broad interpretation is indeed accurate, and our findings involve constructing a fully functional copy-protection scheme for any unlearnable function utilizing only a weak form of unclonable encryption, referred to as one-time sampleable unclonable encryption. In addition, we also establish that a particular type of strong unclonable encryption is essentially equivalent to copy-protection for any unlearnable function, and this equivalence serves as the foundation for the development of a novel, efficient, and secure form of one-time sampleable unclonable encryption.

In this work, a novel framework is introduced that allows the integration of authentication capabilities into existing error-correcting codes, without significantly impacting decoding performance. We demonstrate the creation of an authenticated counterpart for any code with asymptotically negligible coding rate, building upon well-known coding constructs such as polar codes, low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, and simple algebraic codes. For codes without asymptotically negligible rates, we propose an innovative technique to develop an authenticated counterpart with only a minor increase in rate, amounting to $R_{\text{auth}}=R_{\text{base}}+O(N^{-1})$, where $N$ represents the scale factor for the specific class of codes in question. Furthermore, we present practical applications of this technique to well-known codes, including the development of authenticated polar codes and LDPC codes suitable for use in the binary erasure channel. We also examine the trade-off between rate and false-positive error probability in our constructed codes.

We utilize a combination of experimental measurements and theoretical modeling to examine the plasmon characteristics in twisted bilayer MoS$_2$. Our method allows us to generate random lattice configurations and subsequently calculate their electronic properties, even when the twisted structure lacks a well-defined periodicity. We found that lattice relaxations can significantly affect the plasmon behavior, especially in the magnetic phases, and that doping can greatly impact plasmon energies and dispersion, especially in the highly-doped regime near the edge of the MoS$_2$ band structure, where an unusual plasmon band may be controllably created at the Fermi edge through doping adjustment.

In this study, we examine the potential for an almost conformal Ricci soliton to be an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton under the assumption that the almost conformal Ricci soliton's potential vector field is an irreducible gradient field. We provide a necessary and sufficient condition for this condition to be met, and the required condition leads to the classification of the almost conformal Ricci soliton's potential vector field in the case of a Einstein metric. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this scenario is equivalent to having a conformal metric.

The extensive and enduring impact of stellar winds on magnetized stars and planets remains a central theme in research, shaping the upper atmospheres and plasmas of both. Despite distinct differences in size and mass, both stellar and planetary magnetospheres share a common goal: to protect their environments and extend their influence through the flow of plasma. This editorial overviews the varying ways in which wind and magnetic field interactions shape the upper atmospheres and plasmas of stars and planets, with a focus on the interconnected processes that occur at their boundaries, including the formation of current systems, shock waves, and magnetic reconnection. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of these processes is crucial for interpreting the features and fluctuations observed in the upper plasmas of these celestial bodies.

The effect of high-pressure on the Hall scattering is quantitatively examined in a series of Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers with varying Bismuth layer thickness.  The investigation reveals an unusual resistance-hall ratio versus Bismuth thickness curve under both normal and pressurized conditions, with the pressure causing a significant increase in this ratio across all measured Bismuth thicknesses.  This behavior can be attributed to the transition from two-dimensional to three-dimensional electron transport within the Bismuth layers.  The findings also reveal that the Hall scattering mechanism switches from being resistance-dominated at normal conditions to being carrier-dominated under pressure conditions, with this transition occurring when the Bismuth thickness exceeds a certain threshold due to the two-dimensional carrier localization under pressure.

The paper investigates 2-fold scaled fractional N-dimensional time-independent Schrödinger equations under nonlocal scalar potentials, U(x^α) and V(y^α)x^α, where x^α represents x in a space with altered metrics according to α. The term α, a key factor in the equations' definition, determines the impact on U and V, the potential functions, which depends on their locations, in a specific way. For V, the potential's behavior is particularly complex due to its dependence on x's direction. The problem of self-adjointness arises with the potential U(x^α), but it can be resolved with the constraint |x|^α ≤ k, a condition that limits its domain. The paper also obtains the fundamental spectrum for U(x^α), which includes its structure, dimensions, and eigenfunction characteristics, which may be found are directly related to the parameter α. The potential V(y^α)x^α, due to its complexity, requires further investigation, but its self-adjointness can be guaranteed with specific choices of y's domain, a condition that affects the equations' solutions. The paper's final section discusses the impact of its findings on the problem of Toda chains' soliton solutions.

This paper formally proves that a specific type of deep neural network can be trained to achieve optimal generalization performance within a predetermined error margin, regardless of the specific $p$-norm used. We demonstrate that by minimizing the $p$-norm of the input and output vectors, we can obtain a trainer that enforces a bounded Lipschitz constant of up to $R$ on the neural network. Additionally, we show that this results in an optimal generalization error of at least $R^q/n^{1/q}$ for $q$-strong linear learners, where $n$ represents the size of the data set. We further establish that this bound is consistent with the known limits of generalization for linear models and that the required $p$-norm can be as low as $p=2$ for our theoretical bounds to be relevant. We also provide empirical evidence suggesting that models with bounded Lipschitz constants can lead to significant generalization improvements in practice.

Sequential models that utilize local rules to analyze sentence structure may seem
limited by their lack of full sentence understanding at any given moment.
Despite this, these models have achieved significant success in parsing and
semantics, particularly when supplemented with additional resources like
word embeddings.
In our research, we show that sequential models can also make effective use of
local heuristics to capture the hierarchical structure of sentences. We begin by
identifying a critical flaw in the methodology of multiple high-performing
sequential models, where they incorrectly assume that the meaning of a sentence
is closely tied to the meaning of its individual parts. We address this issue
by proposing an alternative evaluation metric, moving beyond the reliance
on machine learning, and making models more resistant to flawed inputs. Our
results demonstrate that simple modifications to the training process of
sequential models can significantly boost their performance on complex sentences,
especially when those sentences contain relative clauses. When tested on real
world data, our findings indicate that models can accurately detect the start
of relative clauses within those sentences.

A planetary system, named HD80606, has a remarkable feature in its sole planet, HD80606b, due to the extreme heat exchange resulting from its close proximity to its host star at its tightest point in orbit. As the planet journeys 43 days around its star, its surface rapidly cools during its distant point in orbit and heats up at its closest point. Despite initial estimates, a re-evaluation of existing data reveals a significantly lower estimated range for the planet's heat exchange rate. Additionally, this re-assessment yields a revised temperature reading for the planet during its closest point in orbit, slightly below 8000 degrees Fahrenheit. It's worth noting that this planet's interactions with its star lead to some interesting effects on the star's light output, allowing for a more precise measurement of the planet's size and shape as it orbits.

Effective gamification boosts motivation during repetitive tasks by providing an engaging balance of effort and interactivity. Conversely, overemphasis on interactivity can lead to idle behavior, negating the therapeutic benefits of physical rehabilitation exercises that are, by necessity, demanding to be effective. We resolute this conundrum by developing a model that theoretically yields optimal rehabilitation outcomes via a precise equilibrium of interactivity and demand, achievable in practice through a straightforward algorithm. We also design a user-friendly, web-based framework that refines this algorithm to accommodate changing performance dynamics during real-world, in-clinic sessions. Results from large-scale user tests validate our approach, demonstrating significant reductions in idle behavior and overall session durations in excess of 30 minutes. Notably, our method proves adaptable to diverse physical therapy applications, as evidenced by successful trials with end-users requiring upper limb rehabilitation following stroke-induced paralysis.

We investigated the optimal strategies for minimizing energy in nonlinear elastic materials with geometrically significant deformations, specifically in plate and rod configurations. By linearising the nonlinear behaviour within a small perturbation framework, we established the connection between the nonlinear material properties and the brittle fracture energies in these structures.

Our study explores the significance of implementing the NLO plus power spectrum (NLO$+$PS) methodology in fixed-order approximate cross-section calculations, specifically for vector leptoquarks within the SU(2)$_L$ $\otimes$ SU(3) $\otimes$ SU(5), in the Standard Model. We develop a set of public tools to compute approximate cross-sections for vector leptoquarks, taking into consideration both their decay into charged leptons and hadronic jets, and derive a set of minimal sensitivity patterns for a range of NLO$+$PS spectrum bins. Furthermore, we provide a detailed description of the design choices underlying our approach, and make the associated code publicly available.

A novel approach using deep neural networks is presented to enhance low-dose PET images in conjunction with MRI data, specifically for pediatric oncology applications. A unique cycle-consistent generative adversarial network is designed to fuse low-dose PET information with high-dose PET data while ignoring the contaminated MRI images, resulting in uncorrupted PET images. Another network uses a U-Net structure to correct contaminated MRI images based on low-dose PET images and actual MRI data. When tested with publicly available data, the proposed framework demonstrated superior performance compared to baseline methods. Consequently, this technique has the potential to reduce the high-dose PET dosages required for pediatric cancer patients, thus minimizing radiation exposure.

Previous studies primarily focused on technical aspects of news personalization, yet they lacked an age-based analysis of users' perceptions of personalized news and their associated privacy concerns. Our research aims to address this gap by exploring how individuals of distinct age groups view the balance between personalized news and privacy. We gathered responses from 1,093 university students across three age brackets: 18-21, 22-28, and 29-45 years old. Each bracket received a customized survey tailored to their proposed personalized news system, which sparked their imagination and motivation for using such a service. Our data analysis revealed significant variations in the preferences, concerns, and willingness-to-pay for personalized news among the different age groups, with the youngest age group being the most open-minded towards data sharing and the oldest being the least accommodating. Notably, the middle age group (22-28 years old) demonstrated the highest willingness-to-pay for personalized news, which surprised us as we had expected the oldest age group to have the highest willingness-to-pay due to their greater life experience. Additionally, our results showed that users' perceived value for personalized news directly correlates with their willingness-to-pay. Furthermore, our findings indicated that users' willingness-to-pay for personalized news is motivated by their desire for up-to-date information and is an indicator of their information overload, which we measured as 'news fatigue'.

This study examines the impact of contemporary contextualized language models on neural coreference resolution systems and their interaction with coreference patterns defined by centering theory. We introduce a new evaluation framework that assesses model performance based on both coreference accuracy and adherence to centering theory guidelines. Our findings reveal that high-performing neural coreference resolution systems tend to deviate from centering principles, but also show that such models can excel in coreference tasks when guided by CT guidelines. Moreover, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of contextualized embeddings like BERT in enhancing coreference resolution accuracy and adapting these models to centering principles further amplifies their effectiveness. However, we also observe that over-reliance on high-quality pre-trained contextualized embeddings can lead to a degree of functional specialization, making them less versatile in tasks that require less coreference-related data.

The concept of treewidth has been successfully applied to developing efficient parameterized algorithms for various types of graphs. While some natural variations of the treewidth parameter are effective for directed acyclic graphs, the well-known parameterized algorithm by Koster, Kiljanenko, and van der Zwaan (2019) still employs the standard treewidth parameter to solve the Directed Feedback Vertex Number problem efficiently. This paper demonstrates that the same problem can be solved efficiently using a narrower parameterized approach called the extended clique-width, which has significant implications for our understanding of the treewidth parameter in directed acyclic graphs. Furthermore, this discovery leads to a treewidth lower bound of at least 4 for 3-edge-outrier weighted directed acyclic graphs, resolving a previous open question by van der Zwaan (2019).

Optimization techniques have a notable influence on modern systems, ranging from computer networks to economic systems, with systems being represented by complex configurations that reflect the optimization principles behind them. To gain insights into these systems, researchers use computational methods to transform the optimization formulation into a compact mathematical form that can be efficiently processed. In this context, we have observed a surge in interest in automated configuration construction using machine learning, but these approaches primarily focus on predictive accuracy, neglecting the human understanding of underlying principles. To address this limitation, we have explored the application of optimization-based methods in learning from complex systems. Our empirical evaluations on three diverse domains--multi-agent reinforcement learning, economic graph optimization, and signal processing--have shown substantial improvements in state representation, generalization, and expert performance metrics. Furthermore, our results indicate that by incorporating optimization learning with low-rank constraints and robust representations, we can achieve better performance, exemplified by a significant reduction in action space dimensions in multi-agent reinforcement learning.

We investigate the long-term behavior of certain operators in the SU(1,1) and SU(2) Lie groups using both exact and approximate methods on finite and infinite systems. Our analysis employs two distinct approaches to calculate the eigenvalues and eigenoperators of these systems under the action of the Hamiltonian. Implementing these techniques using both exact and approximate methods on finite and infinite systems, we demonstrate the onset of asymptotic behavior and precisely determine the rates at which different operator aspects grow in both the finite and infinite system limits. Additionally, we outline the coexistence of distinct asymptotic behaviors within the infinite system context and the related phase transitions.

Range-based device-free sensing utilizes the distance between WiFi access points and mobile devices to track and estimate geospatial activity within an area. However, accurately measuring these distances is a significant challenge due to the inherent nature of wireless communication. While machine learning can enhance device identification and classification, its potential to estimate geospatial distance between WiFi fingerprints has not been thoroughly explored. Our research demonstrates an innovative approach that employs a deep learning model, specifically a Pairwise Multitask Neural Network (PMNN), to correlate WiFi fingerprint data with spatial coordinates and estimate the geospatial distance between them. We compared our approach to conventional methods, including traditional regression techniques and deep learning models, and found that the latency and accuracy of the estimates improved with the use of machine learning. Furthermore, our PMNN approach showed superior performance in estimating the distance between spatial points, achieving a low mean squared error of 1.5 meters, when compared to a baseline of 2.5 meters.

The concept of advanced civilizations being defined by their energy sources' characteristics is expanded upon, categorizing such entities by the type of energy they utilize: zero-energy (I), zero-force (II), low-entropy (III), and high-entropy (IV) civilizations. The focus lies with Type II civilizations that utilize the energy released from stars and other massive objects through supernovae explosions, examining possible detection methods as a supernovae-based "light curve" would offer the civilization a clear, identifiable pattern. By analyzing the possible techniques for discovering these civilizations, the requirements for a suitable detection method are established, involving either finding a correlation between all nearby Type II civilizations or identifying a specific, closely spaced pair that could be a candidate for this type of civilization. Additionally, the challenge of distinguishing a Type II civilization's signal from other astrophysical phenomena is acknowledged. Three detection strategies are proposed to identify these civilizations: analyzing gamma-ray burst patterns to find evidence of a nearby, undetected source; locating pairs of closely spaced, explosive events in the recorded data of supernovae and gamma-ray bursts; and utilizing machine learning to identify patterns of correlated, low-probability events that could indicate a hidden source of energy.

Traditional centralized approaches to monitoring network performance are hindered by their reliance on a single point of failure, rendering them ineffective in detecting violations of service-level agreements in peer-to-peer networks. To address this limitation, our innovative system utilizes P2P technology to distribute monitoring responsibilities, ensuring no single point of failure exists. By leveraging existing overstock detection methods and extending them through new algorithms, our system detects SLA violations efficiently. Specifically, our solution includes: (1) a utility function driven by peer rankings to identify top-performing peers and pinpoint potential violators; (2) a novel algorithm to estimate the peer set's SLA violation probability; (3) a new approach to detect temporary violations; and (4) an improved algorithm for detecting long-term violations by prioritizing peers, reducing computational costs. Experimental results validate our approach, showing better performance compared to alternative methods.

We begin by outlining the potential benefits of energy recovery linacs, specifically their high efficiency and low beam power requirements. However, we also identify potential limitations in their implementation, chiefly related to the interactions between beam and RF systems, which can lead to the formation of coherent enhancement devices and threshold currents that could limit the applicability of future ERLs. In the case of multi-pass ERLs, which are particularly well-suited for particle beam generation, we find that the choice of filling pattern has a significant impact on the equilibrium current and optimal filling power, influenced by the interplay between coherent acceleration and reduction phenomena across different pulse passes. In our analysis, we explore various filling strategies in relation to the design of the RF system and the energy recovery section, presenting examples that illustrate how certain designs might compromise the ideal equilibrium current distribution in favor of higher total current or optimal energy recovery, respectively. Ultimately, we find that strategic design of the filling pattern can mitigate beam-RF interactions and associated threshold currents, yielding significant gains in current and potentially unlocking new applications for future multi-pass ERLs.

Neutron-scattering measurements off protons were carried out at the MASTER+ facility utilizing 0.5-10 GeV electrons and took place between 98 and 688 MeV. A total neutron cross section of approximately 46.4 x 10^-28 square centimeters was found, with an estimated 1 sigma uncertainty of 5.3 x 10^-29 square centimeters. Additionally, double-polarized experiments were conducted between 98 and 395 MeV, yielding no significant deviation from predicted values.

The formation of planetesimals is still shrouded in mystery, and models vary widely depending on the temperature at the heart of the solar system during its formation, which is intensively debated among scientists. A possible clue to solving this mystery lies in the stickiness of small particles, which has a significant impact on the formation of planetesimals. In order to study this, we experimented with changing the composition of particles in a laboratory simulation of the early solar system, with particular focus on how the collision properties of particles changed as the temperature decreased from 1500 K to 50 K. In our research, we discovered a significant increase in the stickiness of particles in very cold samples, which could result in a new thermal constraint on the formation of planetesimals and further narrow the accepted temperature range. In order to study this, we experimented with changing the composition of particles in a laboratory simulation of the early solar system, with particular focus on how the collision properties of particles changed as the temperature decreased from 1500 K to 50 K. In our research, we discovered a significant increase in the stickiness of particles in very cold samples, which could result in a new thermal constraint on the formation of planetesimals and further narrow the accepted temperature range.
