We invite participants to tackle the task of developing innovative methods for
selecting the best hypothesis from a set of alternatives, with their implications
being thoroughly assessed in the context of categorical data. Building upon a
previous challenge, we have expanded its scope to encompass a broader range of
hypothesis selection scenarios, with a distinct focus on utility functions that
guide decisions through quantifiable benefits and losses. To facilitate competition,
we have established three distinct subtasks catering to diverse interest areas,
and have conducted extensive evaluations of the resulting models, carefully selecting
a limited set of top-ranked submissions for further analysis. Notably, several of
these successful approaches have demonstrated comparable or superior performance to
our best-known benchmark methods.

We release a comprehensive new dataset called DiscSense, consisting of 1350 text samples, 780 discourse marker labels and 7800 lexical entries with associated semantic relationships. These labels and relationships are crucial for understanding how context, marked by discourse elements like 'however' or 'likewise', influences semantic changes in language. They also provide a foundation for a long-overdue area of research in natural language processing - the study of discourse-based semantic modifications. To effectively utilize the data in the development of NLP models, we also create various evaluation metrics and a set of carefully-designed tasks at the word, phrase, and sentence levels. These tasks and evaluation metrics represent a starting point for assessing models' capacity to capture the complex discourse-based semantic changes. We include multiple models that have achieved top results on these tasks in our accompanying report. Furthermore, we provide access to both our dataset and evaluation benchmarks through a publicly-available repository.

A theoretical model has been developed to describe the transition from radiative to non-radiative decay in excited Hanauite nanoparticles. Based on this model, the non-radiative energy barrier was calculated to be approximately 0.8 eV, and it was found that this threshold is higher than the energy of green light. Additionally, the model suggests that upon absorption of two photons, energy can overcome this barrier, leading to the creation of a charged defect within the nanoparticle lattice. This defect was identified as a V center, and calculations indicate it has a very low recombination activation energy of around 0.1 eV. It was also found that the V center has a high charge state and can be stabilized with an oxygen anion nearby, forming an F center on an adjacent site.

We introduce an innovative training technique for neural networks that bypasses backpropagation through the utilization of external memory cells to store error values and compute new membrane states via matrix multiplications. This novel approach redefines the way errors are computed, doing away with reverse mode backpropagation in favor of a simplified iterative process. Building upon existing research into neural networks with spiking membranes, our method transforms each membrane neuron into a weighted summation unit identical to those found in traditional artificial neural networks, thus providing a direct, accessible pathway into the underlying mechanics of neural networks through neural dynamics. This modification allows us to build neural networks with spiking membranes using established optimization methods, such as stochastic gradient descent, by simply training the weighted input connections to these membranes. We showcase the efficacy of this training algorithm when applied to neural networks with spiking membranes that utilize a form of synaptic learning known as long-term depression, and we have found it to be superior to existing alternatives, resulting in improved performance on both the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.

We investigate a model that combines a SU(2) Yang-Mills-Higgs theory with a 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole field and a skyrmion field, where the Yang-Mills-Higgs part has a non-trivial homotopy class. By analyzing the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield (BPS) equation, we find that the vortex line, string, and both magnetic skyrmion and monopole can coexist as BPS solutions, depending on the homotopy group of the target space. Furthermore, when the target space has a non-trivial $\pi_1$, both the Yang-Mills-Higgs monopole and the skyrmion can exist as BPS solutions in the Yang-Mills-Higgs monopole background. Additionally, when the target space has a non-trivial $\pi_2$, both the Yang-Mills-Higgs vortex line and string can exist as BPS solutions in the Yang-Mills-Higgs monopole background. When the target space has a non-trivial $\pi_3$, both the Yang-Mills-Higgs monopole and the skyrmion can exist as BPS solutions in the Yang-Mills-Higgs string background.

We investigated how the Hartree-Fock method's convergence is affected by the strength of the electron-electron Coulomb interaction when using the direct SCF technique, and we found that an appropriate initial guess can prevent rapid divergence during the convergence process. Additionally, we observed that weakly interacting electrons require more delicate treatment to converge, and we found that employing a unitary coupled cluster guess can significantly improve convergence rates across various interaction strengths, particularly in tough-to-converge cases where the initial guess leads to rapid divergence.

In this research, we uncover a hidden link between two distinct forms of disorder: structural and dynamical, which can cause a highly unstable and rapid onset of explosive synchronization. This intricate connection is revealed through detailed analytical and numerical investigations of a coupled map lattice with spatially varying and randomly assigned update rules, resulting in highly unpredictable and ever-changing patterns of both local and global dynamics. Our studies demonstrate that the structure of this highly complex system, as embodied by its attractors, can be used to accurately identify and distinguish between two critically important phases: the explosive synchronization phase, characterized by brief periods of highly unstable and rapidly changing behavior, and the regular synchronization phase, characterized by longer periods of stable and predictable dynamics. Additionally, our findings indicate that the relationship between these two phases is heavily influenced by a critical factor: the distance between two highly stable attractors, which separates the two phases and plays a pivotal role in determining the overall dynamics of the system. Our research also uncovers another significant finding, which is that this critical factor is governed by a universal scaling law that is derived from an exhaustive analysis of various parameters and conditions. Lastly, our studies confirm that this scaling law is a fundamental and inherent property of the system, as it holds true even in scenarios where the system undergoes multiple transitions between different forms of synchronization.

We examine a general matrix optimization problem where the objective function can be factored into two sets of variables linked by the matrix product, under specific convexity and smoothness conditions. These conditions are met if the individual components of the objective function satisfy certain properties of strong convexity and smoothness when the factorized form is viewed as a smooth convex function along the geodesic path defined by matrix inversion. We derive a key inequality that establishes the restricted strong convexity of the factorized objective function, and demonstrate that this property holds for specific applications, including the D-optimal condition in linear regression with Gaussian noise. Building on prior work, we obtain an efficient algorithm to solve the general matrix optimization problem within a known error bound, and provide a specific instance of this bound for the D-optimal condition in linear regression.

In 1990, Yang and Yang proposed a conjecture that a bipartite graph with maximum degree 3 can be edge-colored using 4 colors. This conjecture remains unproven to this day. However, research has made significant progress in related areas, such as determining the edge-coloring requirements for planar graphs and double covering graphs. Now, we introduce a new concept called'strong edge-coloring,' which builds upon the idea of edge-coloring. A graph is said to have a strong edge-coloring if its edges can be colored using two different colors, such that no two adjacent edges have the same color and no edge connected to a degree-2 vertex also has the same color. We managed to demonstrate that a bipartite graph with maximum degree 3 or an even maximum degree can be strongly edge-colored using 3 or 2 colors, respectively. Additionally, this result expands our understanding of a broader conjecture related to strong edge-coloring.

This paper presents a novel identity linking Dirichlet L-series with Gauss sums in Chapter 2. A broader context of this identity is provided by a generality involving multiple Dirichlet characters in Chapter 3. Additionally, Chapter 4 demonstrates that a particular identity stemming from this context yields substantial improvements to earlier results concerning the non-vanishing of certain L-functions.

The search for gravitational wave backgrounds generated by the primordial universe can provide significant insights into cosmology. However, if heavy particles were produced in the early universe, they would have a tendency to over-produce gravitational waves at a certain scale, potentially clashing with limits set by particle physics. In this context, new limits on gravitational wave backgrounds have been established at a specific frequency, and these constraints hold a potential for heavy particle physics even if those particles do not directly produce gravitational waves. Furthermore, this study introduces a new method to derive limits on gravitational wave backgrounds by incorporating the effects of primordial black hole formation. In the most favorable conditions, it's possible to place more stringent limits on the spectrum of gravitational wave backgrounds, and this technique can be applied to other models of heavy particle physics. In the case of the scalar field oscillation model, the newly derived limits can forecast the production of primordial black holes, and it's also demonstrated how existing limits on gravitational wave backgrounds can be expressed in terms of the formation of primordial black holes.

We investigate how helical swimmers propel themselves forward in a disordered medium, particularly in a non-unidirectional suspension, and discover a snowman-like effect where the swimmer's motion transitions from rapid forward movement to reversed movement due to long-range force interactions. A mathematical model reveals that the swimmer's behavior is governed by the ratio of its length to the range of the force it exerts, and this can result in the swimmer reversing direction. However, this reversal is only achievable if the force it exerts is weaker than the force it is subjected to.

This study explores how Nash Equilibrium Hamming Distance evolves during the run of a co-evolutionary algorithm, using the OnePlusOne method as an example. We compare two scenarios: a social learning environment where individuals can observe other populations' Hamming Distances, and an individual learning environment where individuals only focus on their own Hamming Distance. Our algorithm seeks to minimize the Bessel function of the first kind, which models the expected Hamming Distance from any starting point. We analyze and graph the Hamming Distance over time in both learning environments to illustrate their differences. Our results show that the Hamkinson Bessel function of the first kind has a significant impact on the convergence of the algorithm. We validate our theoretical findings by conducting multiple runs of the algorithm and collecting statistical data. We also identify the conditions under which the algorithm converges quickly, taking only a few generations, to a tight Hamming Distance range.

The rapid dissemination of information through the internet creates various opportunities for cybercriminals to spread malicious plans. To combat this, it's essential to monitor and track the evolution of these schemes by analyzing online forums' discussions. This task revolves around identifying references to newly introduced malicious plans within discussions posted to online forums, particularly identifying concepts like payment confirmation, phishing, and malware that are relevant to security experts. To address this, we propose a novel approach called the Inter-Sequence Reasoning Model, which incorporates Bidirectional LSTMs to extract contextual information and incorporate it into a Knowledge Distillation framework for accurate concept classification. To improve and fine-tune this model, we introduce a new self-correcting training method called Contrastive Mean Teacher, which yields exceptional results by surpassing the performance of existing techniques. Our experiments demonstrate that both the proposed model and training method excel in both accurate concept extraction and classification, as well as in real-world applications scenarios.

We investigate the dynamics of an Ising model with multiple interacting species on a one-dimensional ring, where each spin can adopt either a "up" or "down" state and may belong to one of two opposing opinions. By updating the system according to specific rules that combine updates typical of the Glauber and Kawasaki dynamics, we find that the resulting system exhibits novel behavior, including both synchronized and diverse states of magnetization. Interestingly, we discover that certain system parameters can produce both periodic and non-periodic orbits of the magnetization. Furthermore, we derive an exact analytical solution for the stationary states of the system and demonstrate that certain stationary state magnetization levels may be destabilized through tiny fluctuations. For large rings, we establish that the system size can be asymptotically disregarded when calculating the stationary state magnetization, revealing that the result is comparable to that of a pure Ising model. Additionally, we provide a precise condition under which the system can exhibit bistability between two different stationary states and this condition aligns with predictions made by a simplified theory. Lastly, we provide a numerical analysis that confirms the theoretical predictions made in this study.

We've developed an efficient model to analyze the spread of COVID-19 through airborne transmission, capturing the influence of droplet sizes, weather conditions, temperature differences, and ventilation rates on infection probability. By incorporating these factors, our model offers a broader understanding of the risks involved in airborne contagion, particularly for high-risk locations and activities, and can provide guidelines for minimizing transmission probabilities through appropriate environmental adjustments. By applying a stochastic search algorithm, we've identified optimal control solutions to reduce infection probabilities in specific environments, and have also established the connection between our model and the epidemic response model, while exploring the implications for policy interventions.

The convergence of neural networks in solving inverse and ill-posed problems has long been misunderstood. While they have successfully tackled various difficult tasks such as image denoising and deblurring, the explanation for their success has yet to be fully captured by a comprehensive theory. In this work, we take a step back from specific techniques such as deep Unrolled networks and Recurrent Residual Learning models, and take an abstract approach to re-examine the neural network's ability to tackle ill-posed problems via iterative refinement. We demonstrate that by introducing an appropriate loss function and a suitable iterative algorithm embedded in the network, any neural network can solve any ill-posed problem, including those that cannot be addressed by traditional methods. We support our findings with concrete mathematical proofs and illustrate our conclusions with empirical studies. We further show that a simple Last Layer (LL) Unfolding method can outperform complex state-of-the-art Unfolding and Unrolling architectures on two challenging image processing tasks, highlighting that neural networks can often achieve impressive results for ill-posed problems by simply minimizing a suitable loss function over the input data set.

This study examines the equalities between ordinary and symbolic powers of edge ideals in weighted oriented graphs, building on the work of Gerber-Haney and Eisenbud-MacEvish in unweighted graphs. The equalities can be derived from a weighted oriented graph to its unweighted counterpart, allowing us to characterize the degree sequences that result in equalities between ordinary and symbolic powers. Additionally, new, non-trivial examples of weighted oriented graphs with equalities between ordinary and symbolic powers are provided, shedding light on the complexity of determining if such equalities hold generally.

A recent study provides explicit formulas for the partition functions of SU(N) and U(N) lattice theories, extending previously known results in 4d to any dimension. These formulas reveal the difference between the SU(N) and U(N) partition functions, showing that the latter can be expressed as a product involving the former. Furthermore, it has been found that certain SU(N) partition functions exhibit polynomial or logarithmic dependence on N, and these dependencies vanish as N approaches infinity. For U(N), the partition functions generally display the same pre-Asymptotic N behavior as their SU(N) counterparts, but with an additional N factor. It is also shown that the difference between the SU(N) and U(N) partition functions can be significant, potentially influencing phase transitions and spontaneous symmetry breaking in the limit of large N.

A critical challenge in utilizing neural networks for critical data security lies in addressing silent data corruptions caused by hardware faults. These corruptions can occur without warning, leading to unpredictable consequences. We present an innovative technique called non-uniform range restriction method, a method for detecting and mitigating silent data corruptions in neural networks. This technique works by limiting the input data range to a specific, error-resistant segment, thereby reducing the risk of corruption. We have developed three distinct variation techniques of this method, including a simple non-uniform data clamping technique, a more efficient technique utilizing linear interpolation, and a sophisticated technique employing regression analysis. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in error resistance, energy efficiency, and system reliability with only minimal performance degradation. Notably, our techniques achieve substantial reductions in error rate across various datasets and neural network architectures.

This paper introduces a novel concept called netting, which can be applied to settle transactions between parties in an economy by combining multiple debt obligations into a single debt. To achieve this, we transform the netting process into a minimum-weight perfect matching problem in a weighted bipartite graph. By leveraging this formulation, we develop a graph-based algorithm to compute optimal netting configurations efficiently. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through analytical and practical evaluations.

In this research, the Generalized Jordanian Twister (GJT) was re-examined by the Regressive Matrix Method (RMM). Initially, the GJT was represented as a product of two simple Jordanian twisters: one in the variable $x$ and the other in the variable $\log x$. A distinct feature of the GJT was its inability to generalize the simple Jordanian twister beyond the degenerate parametric space. The proof demonstrated that the GJT is equivalent to a product of two simple Jordanian twisters and the parameter $h$ can be reabsorbed into one of the twisters. Moreover, this finding implies that the 2-soliton solution of the GJT can be derived from the product of two simple Jordanian twister solitons. The research also uncovered a new simple Jordanian twister whose RMM representation yields the 2-soliton solution, and this new twister can be obtained from the GJT by replacing $h$ with $-h$.

This study tackles the challenge of identifying names in low-resource languages, specifically focusing on adapting high-performance models for improvement. By utilizing parallel data from a related language to fine-tune a high-performance model, we've observed a significant boost in name detection accuracy in the low-resource language. To further enhance this adaptation, we introduced a novel technique incorporating the identified names from the related language into the low-resource language's name tag dataset. This method proved highly effective in comparing data augmentation techniques and resulted in superior performance. Our findings demonstrate that both adapting high-performance models through parallel data and incorporating related-language names lead to substantial gains in name detection F-score, with the latter achieving an F-score of 0.80 or higher in five out of seven evaluated languages.

Our findings based on ALICE's data reveal consistent trends in particle ratios across various collisions, from the smallest (p-Pb) to the largest (Pb-Pb). Specifically, the larger the collision system, the greater the increase in ratios of multi-particle to same-particle types. This pattern is observed for particles such as pions, kaons, and protons. Additionally, when comparing different collision systems for the same particle type, we notice that the increase in ratios correlates with the system's charge-to-system-size ratio. This trend holds true across different centrality measurements and particle types. Furthermore, our data show that the boost in ratios of multi-particle to same-particle types accelerates with increasing system size. This acceleration grows with the energy of the collision. At 2.76 TeV, for instance, the boost in ratios above the baseline value is more pronounced when comparing Pb-Pb collisions to p-Pb collisions than when comparing p-Pb collisions to pp collisions. This phenomenon implies an energy-dependent rise in the effectiveness of multi-particle production relative to single-particle production, especially in larger collision systems at LHC energies.

The presence of flawed labels in datasets significantly hinders the effective training of dialogue state tracking models. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach called Iterative Cost-sensitive Selection (ICS) to eliminate label noise. By designating clean labels as positive samples and recruiting new supporting samples in each iteration, our method efficiently refines the label distribution. The proposed ICS is showcased as a prominent solution among ICS-based methods outperforming the baseline outperforms the baseline in all evaluation metrics, with a notable improvement of 8.35% in the conversational state tracking task in Dialogstate 20. Furthermore, our approach converges quickly with just three iterations, achieving superior performance while significantly reducing the labeling cost.

The intricate interconnectivity of a city's infrastructure and its impact on dynamic systems within it, including the spread of unrest, is not yet fully understood. To better comprehend the effects of different interconnected patterns on dynamic systems, we have developed a generalized mathematical framework that represents a city's infrastructure as a network of interconnected areas. We have also established an applicable simplified model for describing the development of civil unrest, which is influenced by a city's infrastructure and revealed to exhibit diverse patterns of bursty activity at different scales. These patterns emerge naturally due to the specific design of the network, which can also be adjusted manually to reflect various levels of imbalance. Notably, we have discovered that certain network configurations might give rise to similar patterns of bursty activity. Furthermore, we have found that certain dynamic systems, including those generating unrest, typically exhibit short-term memory due to their navigation of the network. We have validated our model with empirical data analyzing the development of unrest in three diverse cities.

Our investigation centered on evaluating the precision of star formation rate (sfr) estimates produced by the Prospector framework, specifically by analyzing  3274 red sequence galaxies from the SDSS with measured Br$\gamma$ luminosities.  We first verified the validity of the $L_{\rm Br\gamma}$-SFR calibration we used, determined at a rate of $5.02\pm0.10\,\$10^{-20}$ \,W.  We then assessed the precision of sfr estimates produced by the Prospector framework via Bayesian inference, including both a standard run with no constraints and a more constrained model that accounted for gas and SFR relationships.  We found a significant correlation between $L_{\rm Br\gamma}$ and SFR, effectively serving as a consistency check for our analysis.  For the standard model, we found a high correlation coefficient of 0.93 between $L_{\rm Br\gamma}$ and SFR, with a moderate precision of 0.11 dex.  Conversely, the more constrained model demonstrated a lower correlation coefficient of 0.83, with a more precise sfr estimate of 0.08 dex.  We also analyzed how $L_{\rm Br\gamma}$-SFR relationships vary based on metallicity, star formation rate, and stellar mass, ultimately determining that these factors do not significantly impact our assessment of sfr precision. We tackle two long-standing challenges in the context of Polynomials Expressible as a Sum of Squares (PEAS). First, we resolve the maximum possible number of squares that can be used in a sum of squares representation for a given polynomial, answering an open question dating back to 1998. This achievement is accompanied by a straightforward, deterministic algorithm identifying a specific number of squares in the expression. The algorithm's success is guaranteed by our investigation into the properties of the Gram matrix within the Gram spectrahedron, particularly its rank. The findings related to this problem serve as a solid foundation for addressing our second PEAS-related challenge: determining the smallest number of squares required to express a given polynomial as a sum of squares. This problem is equivalent to determining the rank of a specific matrix within the Gram spectrahedron. Building upon our previous work, we develop an algorithm to compute this smallest number of squares, along with a specific sum of squares representation, by applying the method of dual problems to the Gram matrix and its submatrices, particularly those with maximal rank within the Gram spectrahedron.

The FASERν experiment at the CERN facility, set to run during T7 and T8 data taking periods of LHC, aims at studying neutrino interactions through the search for monojets and tau neutrinos and through event number measurements of other neutrino flavors. With its unique location, it can make distinct contributions to our understanding of leptonic non-unitarity, complementing existing constraints on CKM non-unitarity. Our analysis indicates that, with 5 ab−1 of integrated luminosity, the experiment can place meaningful upper limits on deltapm and gamma, even if the LHC runs at its nominal energy of 13 TeV. Furthermore, in the case of 100 TeV run with 3 ab−1 of integrated luminerty, the experiment can reach upper limits of order 0.1 for these parameters, significantly enhancing our current knowledge in this area.

Brzozowski's operator has been adapted to create an efficient symbolic method for evaluating whether one regular expression fully contains another. This technique's effectiveness relies heavily on the ability to compute the derivative of a regular expression, a fundamental operation that is proven correct and efficient for our proposed extended language. Our work also includes a method for determining if one regular expression can be minimized to another, along with implications for automaton evaluation. This research builds upon Brzozowski's work and extends it to our new parameters, resulting in a usable and efficient system for automaton evaluation and containment checking.

Deep learning-based Visual-Inertial Odometry models have excelled in recent years, surpassing traditional VIO algorithms in complexity and accuracy. While these deep learning-based VIO models have successfully applied deep learning principles to process both visual and inertial data, there are varying approaches in use. This diversity in methods is an obstacle to advancing VIO technology through further deep learning optimization. To move forward, this study aggregates multiple deep learning-based VIO models, integrating their algorithms into a unified framework that utilizes recurrent neural networks to combine visual and inertial information. This framework significantly outperformed traditional VIO algorithms and even the individual models it was derived from.

We investigate a recently discovered phase, double-Weyl semimetals, which are three-dimensional equivalents of Dirac points in two dimensions, and uncover their unique "square-root" topology. By paring two Weyl points with opposite charges, we find that the resulting material exhibits double-Weyl behavior, featuring linear dispersion along two direction and quadratic dispersion along the third direction in its bulk form. We classify double-Weyl semimetals based on this understanding and propose that they can be created through the application of chemical pressure to Weyl semimetals, which would result in double-Weyl points forming near the Fermi level only if the pressure direction lies within a specific, directionally-restricted area. Moreover, we propose that pair-breaking processes are necessary for stabilizing double-Weyl semimetals and outline several potential materials science approaches to realize this phase experimentally.

This study examines the effectiveness of edge finite elements in solving a fundamental data completion problem involving the Poisson equation. Specifically, we investigate how different edge finite element methods handle partial data to recover missing information on the Dirichlet boundary. Our analysis focuses on a specific case where the discrete solution is defined by edge finite elements with minimal degree, and we explore both locally irregular and smooth solutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's ability to accurately recover both small and large domain solutions, and our findings highlight the significance of carefully selecting edge finite elements to achieve optimal results.

This paper delves into the properties of the parafermion vertex operator algebra (VOA) associated with the affine Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, for which we determine the irreducible modules and construct the Fourier-Mukai transform for VOAs. Furthermore, we establish the connection between the parafermion VOA and the lattice VOAs constructed from $A_n$ lattices, and prove the simplicity of certain self-extensions of the vacuum module for $osp(1|2n)$, for $n \geq 4$.

We introduce a novel perspective on training a student model that utilizes
saliency to identify and focus on the knowledge from an experienced model,
addressing an unresolved challenge in the knowledge amalgamation framework.
Unlike existing approaches that rely on computationally expensive adversarial methods
to pinpoint knowledge gaps, our solution leverages a simple yet robust technique
to determine the most crucial portions of the expert model.
By combining these key elements with initial student knowledge, we achieve
remarkable improvements in the efficiency of the training process.
Our method showcases exceptional performance on both the minimalistic
FedCAML and the more complex settings, showcasing significant boosts
in accuracy and a marked decrease in communication efficiency.

Previous research suggested that grid cells contribute to the brain's internal spatial map, with alternating periodic patterns facilitating location recognition within environmental surroundings. However, a problem persists in understanding how the unique characteristics of grid cells adapt to accommodate external cues such as visual information that significantly alters local environments. Our findings indicate that the unique periodic patterns of grid cells in the rat brain's parietal cortex can shift in response to visual environment changes, going from matching local periodic patterns in open spaces to adapting to confined spaces' patterns. This adaptation is achievable through the rat's internal spatial map learning to override external influences through salience-based learning, thus allowing efficient location recognition across varying environments.

The development of stable magnetic fields in small, slowly rotating stars like M-dwarfs remains poorly understood. These stars likely generate magnetic fields through kinematic dynamo processes, which can produce transient patterns of magnetism. The issue then becomes explaining how these stars can develop magnetic cycles in time, given that kinematic dynamos typically produce short-lived magnetic fluctuations. In this study, we investigate whether adding convective turbulence to turbulent thermal dynamos could lead to the creation of stable magnetic regions and cycles in small, slowly rotating stars. Our model includes realistic descriptions of convection and turbulent thermal forces, treated using the multi-component turbulent dynamo theory. We find that turbulent thermal forces play a crucial role in maintaining magnetic regions and cycles in these stars, and that the heat deposited by turbulent thermal forces at magnetic boundaries is sufficient to support stable magnetic regions. Furthermore, we find that this process results in long-lived magnetic fluctuations in stars with rotational periods longer than 20 days, and that this could explain the observed relationship between rotation and magnetic cycle periods in M-dwarfs.

We start by listing all S4 quartic extensions in rational fields of characteristic not 2 or 3, then analyze a diverse set of elliptic curves defined over these fields, establishing that many curves do not gain rank when extended to these fields. In particular, of the 48,000+ possible S4 quartic extensions, we identify around 476 that satisfy specific conditions, such that a vast majority (around 98%) of their rational points remain confined to the original field, when considering not just elliptic curves but also a broader class of analytic objects defined by Horohay. When extending fields to S4, certain elliptic curves retain the same rank, but this phenomenon is rare, occurring in less than 1% of cases. Building on this understanding, we are able to prove a more general theorem about the density of ranks in elliptic curves over rational S4 extensions, concluding that a particular set of curves with GL2-action on hermitian spaces of weight 2 exhibits scalar rational densities equivalent to those found in the broader S4 context.

We investigate the time-dependent production of entropy in a system that undergoes sudden changes, specifically those associated with quantum quenches. Our analysis focuses on the total entropy, as well as the irreversible and heat entropies, within the equilibrium and nonequilibrium frameworks described by the 1D XY chain's XXX+XYY model. Our study utilizes an exact Bethe ansatz solution to derive time-dependent expectations and cumulants of the total, irreversible, and heat entropies through the imaginary time formalism. We examine the system's behavior both before and after the quantum quench, looking at different initial states and conditions that vary in temperature, irreversibility, and heat. We found that certain quantum quenches can result in an increase in entropy that slows down over time, while also producing heat that speeds up as it loses intensity. Additionally, we discovered that some quench states can be identified as thermodynamic states represented by high-temperature equilibrium states, and that such states can occur when the Hamiltonian's ground state is nondegenerate. Moreover, we found that certain quantum quenches can produce an initial spike in the production of irreversible entropy, accompanied by a heat entropy that rises in contrast. We also found that the heat entropy speed-up phenomenon is linked to the system's return to an equilibrium state characterized by a high rate of heat transfer.

We investigate the long-term behavior of a system interacting with an environment, specifically the time-twirling of the combined state over all time. It's demonstrated that its trace distance from equilibrium represents a form of "distinguishability time" that caps at the system's decoherence time. This concept is applied to various scenarios, including quadratic dissipation, quantum Brownian motion, and Lindblad dynamics, where we derive an upper limit on distinguishability time. Notably, we find that this time eventually reaches a steady-state value, and it's also related to the entropy growth of the system over time. In particular, in the case of quadratic dissipation, it's shown that the trace distance from equilibrium divides the time-axis into two distinct domains, and it's argued that this behavior could have implications for the coexistence of system and environment in non-unitary dynamics.

We investigate the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex within the unit cube in n-dimensional space, specifically within the set of points that interpolate to zero at a set of given nodes. Our analysis reveals that for such a simplex to be nondegenerate, the number of interpolation nodes must equal or exceed (n^d)/2 + n, where d represents the dimension of the space. This conclusion surpasses a prior finding and holds the implication that in two-dimensional space, even a single additional node is enough to create an interpolating simplex, even one that is degenerate. Further, we have found evidence to suggest that in higher-dimensional spaces, a similar relationship may also be true, although this requirement may be sufficient, rather than necessary.

The objective of this study was to examine hydrogen distribution in etched silicon devices.  We have demonstrated significant carrier concentration increases in etched silicon, ranging from 1 x 10^17 to 8 x 10^18 per cubic centimeter, depending on etching time and oxide thickness.  A correlation was found between carrier concentration and hydrogen content in etched silicon, and it was observed that etched silicon has a higher hydrogen concentration than etched oxide.  We have also determined that the n+ region in etched silicon has a higher resistance than the n+ region in etched oxide, and that etched silicon has a higher leakage current than etched oxide.  In addition, we have found that the breakdown voltage in etched silicon is lower than in etched oxide.  We have established that etched silicon can cause errors in magnetic field measurements, and that etched oxide does not have this effect.  We have developed methods for reducing hydrogen introduction during the etching process and reducing the size of etched areas.  We have also established that replacing the etched oxide with grown oxide can reduce hydrogen introduction during the etching process.  We have reduced the carrier concentration in etched silicon from 4 x 10^18 to 2 x 10^18 per cubic centimeter by reducing the size of the etched areas.  We have demonstrated that reducing the size of the etched areas can reduce the size of the n+ region in etched

This paper confirms the implications of cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted homotopy K-theory, confirming a prediction made by Kahn and Lipshitz in their paper 'Twisted topological smoke and mirrors'. Additionally, we demonstrate that cdh descent for twisted topological Hochschild homology follows from a more general statement involving topological Hochschild homology and its derivation, and further establish a connection between cdh descent and twisted topological smoke and mirrors.

The dynamic exchange of mass between a planet's interior and exterior can drive profound evolutionary changes in planetary systems, particularly regarding volatile elements. This conceptual framework builds upon existing frameworks like core-accretion and outward diffusion models. The paper contemplates various processes that could facilitate the transfer of elements between a planet's interior and its surrounding environment, encompassing atmospheres, interplanetary medium, exospheres, and heliospheric magnetic connections. It further speculates that recurring or persistent interactions between planets and their environments could significantly impact element cycling, influencing geochemical processes and affecting the long-term atmospheric composition. In the case of terrestrial-like planets located within habitable zones around G-type stars, it is argued that element cycling might counterbalance the distinguishing effects of interior and exterior processes, potentially leading to diverse and stable planetary conditions. Ultimately, the paper suggests that element cycling might underlie several observed correlations between planets and their host stars, and that it holds valuable insights for better understanding the evolution of planetary systems and the evolution of planets themselves.

Our calculations using density functional theory reveal that 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PDO) possesses an activation energy barrier for the conversion to methyl cations that is significantly lower than the analogous barrier in 1,3-propanediol (1,3-PDO). To comprehend the distinct reactivity patterns in these isomers, we conducted an in-depth structural and energetic analysis of the potential energy surfaces of 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO, incorporating the effects of computational method and level of theory. Our study demonstrates that both the initial activation energy barrier and the energy requirements for the conversion to methyl cations in 1,2-PDO are reduced due to the presence of an intramolecular hydrogen bond that facilitates proton transfer, whereas this bond has no significant impact on the potential energy surface in 1,3-PDO. As a result, 1,2-PDO is anticipated to be an efficient and cost-effective alternative to 1,3-PDO for the production of methyl cations in mass spectrometry, without the need for prior functionalization.

Tensor networks, which include matrix product states and PEPS, serve as fundamental resources for studying the behavior of quantum many-body systems. These networks facilitate simulations of static and dynamical properties by retaining only the most significant aspects of the wavefunction. Despite their utility, tensor networks are generally difficult to visualize and extract information from. In quantum circuit learning, unitary quantum circuits can be trained to reproduce observables' behavior, but their utility is limited when dealing with complex many-body systems. Our work overcomes these constraints by introducing an approach to map tensor networks to parametrized quantum circuits in a systematic way. We leverage this mapping to speed up the learning process of quantum circuit networks (QCNs) by bypassing the need for direct interaction with the tensor network during training. Instead, we train a circuit to replicate the network's behavior under unitary transformations, significantly reducing the required resources while achieving comparable accuracy. Our strategy exhibits a trade-off between runtime and the complexity of the tensor network, and we provide a theoretical analysis of this relationship. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that this approach yields substantial computational gains without compromising on the tensor network's entanglement properties. We empirically validate our method using both random and realistic models of quantum systems, showcasing that our technique outperforms the current state-of-the-art in learning from tensor networks while achieving comparable accuracy. Our method has the added benefit of enabling the efficient training of tensor networks by treating the circuit as the primary trainable entity. This innovative strategy could also

The accurate and efficient classification of cancer tissues relies heavily on
the classification of tissue sections, which can be time-consuming and prone to
errors when performed by pathologists manually. To address this challenge, the
analysis of whole-slide images has emerged as a superior alternative. In this
context, cutting-edge techniques like graph neural networks have exhibited great
potential in classifying cancer tissues and detecting disease boundaries.
However, current approaches that combine graph neural networks and multi-task
learning still face issues such as an optimizable learning schedule and the
lack of effective graph construction methods, resulting in a reliance on fixed
learning rules and crude image features that do not do justice to the capabilities
of graph neural networks. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces an
advanced framework called End2End GNN, which employs neural networks to construct
graphs and learn optimal loss functions at each training iteration to achieve
optimal results in both cancer classification and boundary detection. The new
approach was evaluated using 3000 images from two public datasets and outperformed
existing state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin in both tasks.

This paper introduces an advanced random network model called the nonlinear Hawkes process, a generalization of the standard Hawkes process that captures interactions within a complex network of dependent events. We discuss the issues of estimating and validating its parameters under realistic conditions, exploring various techniques such as maximum likelihood estimation, a local score approach for small systems, and statistical testing for specific characteristics. We also examine different simulation-based methods for calculating critical values of critical value functions of the nonlinear Hawkes process. These methods involve using the true parameter values, which are often unavailable in practice. We propose an alternative way to approximate these values by introducing a small perturbation in the parameters and leveraging the linearized properties of the process. We provide theoretical justification for one such approximation method. We use the proposed methods on a small system and an American airline flight schedule data sets.

We introduce a revised implementation of the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) to accelerate the computation of gravitational interactions in N-body simulations, particularly tailored for highly extended and sparse systems characteristic of astrophysical applications. Our approach optimizes FMM's exponential time scaling by leveraging sparse matrix operations, thereby reducing memory usage and execution time. This improvement becomes particularly significant in scenarios to come, where real-time or near-real-time performance will be crucial due to massive data sets and advanced visualization techniques. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through FMM's application to a protostar scenario, where our efficient implementation produces accurate results, maintains overall stability, and achieves substantial speed gains compared to traditional methods, especially for wide-scaled simulations.

Integrating knowledge from one domain of anatomy to facilitate segmentation in another domain is particularly complicated due to significant differences in anatomical structures between domains. This cross-domain adaptation challenge can be addressed through a contrastive semi-supervised learning approach known as CSCADA. The key components of the proposed method include: (1) introducing contrastive learning to incite the separation of similar cross-domain samples and the convergence of far-away points; (2) employing a multi-domain contrastive learning approach to integrate cross-domain information and reduce the gap between them; (3) leveraging a semi-supervised learning technique known as prototypical learning to conduct cross-domain segmentation and refine the adaptation. By combining these strategies, CSCADA achieves superior performance when compared to current state-of-the-art methods for the public MIO challenge dataset.

We provide an explanation for achieving a coherent comprehension of 4D, N=1 supergravity through a revised perspective on the fundamental principles of supergravity, centered around the concept of improved BRS symmetry. By incorporating an improved BRS algebra into the supergravity framework, it is possible to derive the correct BRS symmetry for the supergravity multiplex of the Einstein-Hilbert action. This involves making a specific adjustment to the BRS transformation of the gravitino field, which results in the disappearance of the nilpotent property of the BRS transformation of the gravitino's auxiliary component. This revised approach enables the incorporation of non-abelian gauge theories into supergravity, and we offer some general guidelines for doing so. We also present an adapted BRS algebra for the Einstein-Hilbert action in the context of 4D N=1 supergravity, and demonstrate how anti-commuting vector currents can be used to build consistent BRS representations. Furthermore, we outline the principles of consistent BRS reduction in 4D N=1 supergravity, and provide an example of how to obtain a non-supersymmetric gravity theory through BRS reduction from 4D N=1 supergravity.

In a stellarator, a plasma waveplate can generate long-lived, large-scale magnetic fluctuations known as geodesic accidents (GAs) by converting plasma waves into magnetic fluctuations in a chaotic direction. However, creating functional plasma waveplates that can efficiently produce GAs in future devices like W7-X and Wendelstein 7-0 by converting magnetic fluctuations will require a deeper understanding of the relationship between plasma electron density, magnetic field strength, and waveplate thickness. This understanding is the focus of the research described in this report, which shows that even a thin waveplate can effectively convert long-wavelength GAs if its thickness is much smaller than its wavelength. This thickness constraint can be mitigated by using a magnetic fluctuation waveplate, which can produce long-wavelength GAs even in the absence of a plasma waveplate. These fluctuations have the same purpose as traditional plasma waveplates and can convert magnetic energy from low-frequency fluctuations like the interchange mode instability, often produced by devices like Wendelstein 7-X during low-power operations.

We examine the electric dipole moment of the tau lepton within the type-II two-Higgs doublet extension of the Standard Model, focusing particularly on the CP-violating phase that contributes to this quantity's magnitude. Utilizing unitarity bounds and the stability of the vacuum, we establish a minimum criterion for the ratio of the two Higgs doublet masses. Furthermore, we identify the currently most constraining limit on the ratio of the two Higgs doublet masses from the Standard Model parameters, specifically the W boson coupling to the Higgs boson, and determine that at 95% confidence, this ratio must be greater than or equal to 0.89. We then explore the potential for the tau electric dipole moment to surpass its present experimental limit of $4.1 \times 10^{24} e\cdot\mathrm{cm}$ by several orders of magnitude, finding that this could occur if the ratio of the two Higgs doublet masses is less than about 1.4, with only a limited range of possible values for this ratio.

This paper delves into rank-metric codes, specifically examining the unique error-correcting capabilities they offer in the context of the Hamming metric. We establish criteria for codes to accurately detect and correct errors of various weights in the Hamming metric, building on existing rank-metric distance distribution formulas. These criteria enable us to distinguish between the error-correcting capabilities of codes for rates below and above 1/2, with above 1/2 being more capable. We further analyze specific examples, including quadratic residue codes, to demonstrate their error-correcting performance and optimal decoding strategies. These strategies can be applied to any code with a suitable generator matrix, facilitating the generation of codes with optimal rank-metric error-correcting properties for any desired rate.

This paper provides the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator interpretation of the conserved current block operator in 2-dimensional conformal field theory, and shows that this expression is equivalent to the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation of the same block, but with the conformal block's Casimir operator acting instead on the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator. As a result, we are able to derive the representation of the stress tensor block operator using AdS$_3$ geodesic operators, and confirm its agreement with the semi-classical holographic stress tensor reconstruction method.

We utilized the $35^{th}$ IDPS meeting to present preliminary findings contrast neural network-based autoencoders with traditional methods such as the harmonic transform and vector harmonic transform for reconstructing gravitational lensing, specifically multi-scale neural network, harmonic net and vector net. Our analysis revealed that harmonic net and vector net demonstrated comparable performance to traditional methods and both could serve as viable alternatives due to their superior scalability. Moreover, our results showed that the amplitude spectrum of neural network-based methods contains valuable information on mass distribution at different scales, which is an interesting observation worthy of further research.

In 2001, David Eisenbud, Shihoko Yokura, and others extended the theorem of Gelfand and MacPherson to a more general form applicable to combinatorial differential manifolds. A key aspect of this extension involved the use of a specific total order for the vector spaces. Despite its significance, the order itself was not considered part of the combinatorial data. This paper relaxes this restriction by allowing any order that is compatible with the differential structure, resulting in a more general version of the Gelfand-MacPherson theorem. Additionally, this variant is relevant to the study of critical points in combinatorial optimization problems.

The Type II supernova SN~2020jfo had unusually high levels of iron-peak elements like nickel, iron, and chromium, along with a distinctive absorption line in the near-infrared spectrum indicating the presence of manganese. By comparing its spectra to those of other supernovae, especially SN~2018ivc and SN~2019jc which also exhibited high iron levels, we found that SN~2020jfo behaved differently in its early stages. SN~2020jfo's spectrum in the near-infrared showed a distinct $\lambda$-transition line of manganese, absent in the other two supernovae, and its spectra in the optical range had higher levels of nickel, iron, and chromium, exceeding those of SN~2018ivc and SN~2019jc by five to ten times the error margins. These findings suggest that SN~2020jfo had a significant enhancement of nickel production, resulting in a considerable overabundance of nickel relative to iron, in contrast to our sun's nickel-to-iron ratio. By analyzing light curves and estimating explosion energy releases, we found that SN~2020jfo's explosion with extremely high iron levels might be linked to the collapse of a massive star which produced a compact remnant, probably a black hole, and resulted in a substantial release of energy during the explosion.

A type of high-efficiency lobster-eye (LE) optics, featuring a cross-like image, has complex characteristics that depend on the orientation of its rotation angle. To efficiently analyze this optics system, we propose dividing it into four distinct sections based on an azimuthal rotation angle of 45 degrees. Each section's efficiency is then individually tracked as the LE optics is adjusted. Our data shows that one segment contributes significantly to collecting light, with an optical transfer function resembling a traditional LE optics. Another segment, with a rotation angle of 45 degrees, collects a substantial amount of light but with lower efficiency. Our analysis also identifies potential applications for the other two segments, despite their lower efficiency. To optimize the system, we suggest using a sub-optics element specific to each segment.

We employ level set methods in conjunction with technique adaptations from Hamilton-Jacobi equations and mean curvature flows to analyze and approximate solutions to second-order fully nonlinear partial differential equations. Specifically, we demonstrate the introduction of an auxiliary function within these methods enables the derivation of an equation whose solution can be determined through a first-order linear partial differential equation, ultimately enabling the determination of level set equations. These level set equations may be solved numerically, yielding an implicit representation of the solution to the original fully nonlinear equation. We also establish the convergence of these approximate solutions to the desired solution as the method's discretization parameters approach zero.

We investigated how employing pressure-only models affects the prediction of halo mass in a set of cosmological simulations that feature a distinct, overdetermined structure at the $k_\sw$ scale.  Our analysis centered on a parameter space in which the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations was varied between 0.788e-5 and 8.8e-5.  Notably, we discovered that using pressure-only models results in an inaccurate prediction of halo mass, with a typical error of 0.06 in log mass units.  This mistake became more pronounced as the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations increased in density-only simulations.  Our analysis revealed a clear link between the growth of structure and the inaccuracy in halo mass prediction, with the largest errors observed at $z=0$.  Furthermore, we found that even in the presence of moderate levels of perturbations, pressure-only models failed to accurately capture the characteristics of halo mass, with typical errors of 0.04 in log mass units.  Over time, we noticed that the discrepancy between pressure-only and full physics simulations gradually decreased as the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations increased in density-only simulations.  This behavior was consistent with the findings of previous studies.  Additionally, we found that using the power spectrum of matter density or the linear power spectrum of density and pressure does not differ significantly in simulations conducted with full or pressure-only physics.  Nevertheless, there was a notable distinction in the power spectrum of hal

Our research introduces a pioneering approach to matrix factorization for piano transcription, a semi-supervised version of the Convolutional Neural Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method. Building on CNMF's solid foundation in low-rank factorization and utilization of piano-specific structural information, we enhance it by integrating sparse regularizers and incorporating limited labeled data through an alternating direction method. The modified version, called semi-supervised CNMF (ssCNMF), aims to minimize both the rank of factors and the number of nonzero elements in the sparse matrix, resulting in a more compact and robust transcription model. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ssCNMF surpasses top-performing low-rank factorization techniques and surpasses supervised deep learning methods for piano transcription in both melody extraction and multi-instrument transcription tasks, especially when confronted with noisy and complex inputs.

This research introduces a novel approach to assigning properties like mass, specific angular momentum, and energy to individual fluid elements within stars that rotate. Unlike conventional methods, this approach occurs naturally when using the Eulerian reference frame. By re-expressing the Eulerian reference frame's equations in a way that incorporates the conservation of angular momentum, we derive a set of localized equations that can be used to study rotating stars, particularly those with barotropic and rigid rotation properties, and demonstrate how this leads to the development of a preferred reference frame that aligns with the star's rotation.

A key challenge in using machine learning models lies in acquiring comprehensive and accurately labeled data. Selective labeling addresses this issue by allocating labels to the most informative instances, thereby making the most of limited labeling resources. Despite the theoretical benefits of selective labeling, the practical application remains unclear due to the absence of established methods to identify the best instances for labeling. This study introduces a novel approach to select the top instances for labeling, combining both learning and instance selection, by leveraging a new algorithm that effectively identifies the best instances by prioritizing data efficiency during the labeling process. Experimental results show that this approach leads to significant improvements in the performance of the model on the target task compared to traditional labeling methods.

The discovery of neutron star mergers producing both gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation marks a new era in multi-messenger astronomy. A key challenge now lies in interpreting the complex electromagnetic signals from these events. Our analysis focuses on a neutron star merger observed through gravitational waves and in the form of ultra-high energy cosmic rays, which may have originated from neutron star mergers producing high-energy particles. This work presents a theoretical framework for modeling electromagnetic radiation resulting from interactions between high-energy particles and interstellar gas along the merger path. By utilizing a 1D hydrodynamic approach, we account for the electromagnetic radiation emitted from relativistic particle collisions with gas for both low and high density environments, and even considers the emergence of electromagnetic signals from reaccelerated particles after mergers that produce highly energetic particles. By calibrating our model with simulated relativistic heavy ion collisions, our theoretical framework provides a basis for predicting electromagnetic signatures associated with neutron star mergers producing high-energy particles, and could also be applied to similar astrophysical phenomena like supernovae and black hole mergers.

This paper proposes a multi-task learning framework that utilizes deep learning to extract data from clinical notes and incorporate findings into a health inequality model. Constrained optimization techniques are applied to impose limitations on model complexity and ensure consistency with established inequality measures. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through synthetic experiments and real-world applications utilizing clinical data from the MIMIC-III database. Collabora, a publicly accessible dataset for extracting medical information from clinical notes, is also introduced and used for both model evaluation and comparison with baseline methods.

Our research focuses on modeling a swimmer that can transition between two states in a viscous fluid, with the aim of determining the most efficient path to move it between two fixed locations. We've developed a general framework to analyze this problem, and and by applying asymptotic methods, we've derived simpler formulas that provide valuable insights into how switching frequency affects the cost of moving the swimmer. These formulas help confirm the existence of an optimal switching pattern that minimizes costs, and we've discovered how variations in fluid dynamics influence the performance of different swimming styles. Additionally, we've established conditions under which the most efficient swimming technique involves switching frequently, and we've developed a criterion to predict this optimal switching behavior.

Our analysis of an online platform that facilitates in-person encounters in major US cities during the pandemic reveals significant shifts in diversity from March 2020 to April 2021, with implications for community resilience in the long term. Despite restrictions being lifted by late summer 2020, reduced participation and new barriers to entry persisted, with lingering effects in 2021. Consequently, the diversity of encounters didn't fully recover to pre-pandemic levels until autumn 2021. Additionally, the prolonged decline in new users during the pandemic had a lasting impact on diversity in 2021, with long-term consequences for community resilience. Furthermore, our data show that diversity measures correlated with one another in unexpected ways, with certain measures exhibiting a permanent shift in 2021, for example, the greater representation of women in 2021. Our methodology involves leveraging the diversity-entropic framework to analyze diversity metrics over time, with a particular focus on the variety of new versus established participants.

The intense migration of objects in circumstellar discs surrounding high mass young stars can lead to the formation of a dynamic and unstable inner disc, characterized by rapid object migration and object-object interactions. The study presented here explores how the distribution of objects in this environment evolves as they migrate the full extent of the disc, interacting with one another and experiencing gravitational influence from their host star. The research focuses specifically on a scenario where objects are migrating in a quasi-stable, two-dimensional disc, located within a large, three-dimensional space surrounding a 10 solar mass star. The study reveals a distinct, exponential pattern in the concentration of objects as they migrate towards the star, located at the center of the disc, and further explores how the extent of this concentration is affected by the presence of additional objects, their mass, and their overall migration pattern.

Given an asymptotic algebra at the past, we construct local and asymptotic fields, along with a scattering matrix, which encapsulates the asymptotic relations between these fields. This construction is the foundation of a scattering theory. Ultimately, it is shown that for a given asymptotic algebra, there is exactly one scattering theory, thereby demonstrating that the 2-dimensional scattering theory is uniquely determined by the asymptotic algebra. Additionally, for a given asymptotic algebra with non-trivial scattering matrix, we can recover the underlying field and local fields that define the scattering theory.

Previous 4G and 5G cellular exposures have been compared, revealing a notable difference in radiation levels originating from 5G towers when buildings are factored in. Our study aims to build upon this comparison by assessing exposure limits in both line-of-sight and obstructed environments, taking into account the higher operating frequencies of 5G and potential increased power density. Given the higher power densities of 5G, our research involves conducting numerical evaluations to ensure these densities remain within safety limits when considering various environmental obstacles. In line-of-sight conditions, our analysis shows that 5G exposures surpass those of pre-5G technology. Conversely, in obstructed environments, where buildings and terrain impede signals, our simulations indicate that 5G exposures are significantly lower than those of pre-5G technology. To validate our numerical findings, measurements were taken at multiple 5G and pre-5G cellular sites in both line-of-sight and obstructed environments. Our results indicate that, to meet exposure limits, the power density of 5G operating in line-of-sight modes can be as much as 10 times higher than necessary when operating in obstructed environments. Conversely, pre-5G technology, with lower frequencies, can meet exposure limits in line-of-sight conditions but often exceeds limits in obstructed environments, necessitating signal boosting to meet limits.
